descent-lift.imported-taxonomy-type-p-ru.formal: Every zero divisor of a nondegenerate real Clifford algebra is annihilated on each side by a nontrivial idempotent; in a simple algebra the idempotent is non-central and the obstruction is type P, refined to type N exactly when the annihilating idempotent is $wv$ for a hyperbolic pair $(v, w)$ of null vectors, $vw + wv = 1$. Step 2 of the algorithm diagnoses by three tests in order: a vector of square zero is type N; a central idempotent is type C; otherwise type P, with the caution that nilpotence alone does not diagnose N. Step 3 adjoins a hyperbolic plane for type N, one generator for type C, and nothing for type P, the identity being the repair of an idempotent; a general type-P element has von Neumann pseudo-inverses, and among the idempotents with a given image the self-adjoint one is canonical exactly where a definite form is available. In the $(1,1)$ ascent the adjoined ladder pair $f, f^{*}$ and its occupation projectors are a system of matrix units, the adjoined pair is itself null, and the reflection in an adjoined direction is an automorphism of the ascent. \emph{Provenance:} \cite[Def.~3.1, Ex.~3.5, Thm.~3.9, Thm.~4.2, Rem.~5.8, Prop.~6.1, Rem.~6.6, Thm.~7.1, Prop.~7.8, Table~1]{ButlerT1}.

Every failure is pinned to an element that equals its own square, the three kinds are told apart by simple tests, and the prescribed repair is a new plane, one new direction, or nothing at all. It also records some facts about the smallest enlargement that the note goes on to use.

__notes__.note.descent-lift.setting-what-does-two-: \textbf{One fact.} The root paper proves that the descent is one-way at the level of algebras: no homomorphism returns. The singularity paper premises that the completion supplies no generator off-diagonal in the joint number basis, and its own envelope corollary shows that one pairing rotation is what the return of its boundary modes needs. Proposition \claimref{descent-lift.within-supplied-dynamics-descent-has-no} joins the two: inside the dynamics the framework supplies, the descent cannot be lifted, and the missing ingredient is a pairing rotation, on the adjoined rungs or on the modes themselves. The one-way door and the pairing exclusion are the same statement seen from the two sides of the descent.

\textbf{Whether the principle produces the pairing.} A second registered experiment, deposited as \cite{ButlerPreregT05pairing}, asks the converse question: does the root paper's own procedure, run on the pairing creator, produce the rotation that T5 excludes? The root paper has no element-level completion of a non-invertible element: its no-go theorem closes that route for null vectors, its type-N repair acts on points, and its type-P rule is that nothing is adjoined \cite[Thm.~4.2, Prop.~6.1]{ButlerT1}. What can be run is the six-step algorithm \cite[Table~1]{ButlerT1}.
__notes__.note.transport.setting-refuted-conjectur: An exact inverse being impossible (Lemma \claimref{transport.noinverse}), the standard weakening is a \emph{von Neumann pseudo-inverse}: an element $\sigma(v)$ with $v\,\sigma(v)\,v = v$. Pseudo-inverses of null vectors exist in abundance, since any null partner $w$ with $v \cdot w = \tfrac12$ supplies one by $v^2 = w^2 = 0, \qquad vw + wv = 1, \qquad \text{hence} \quad vwv = (1 - wv)v = v$, so the substantive question is not existence but \emph{canonicity}: can a pseudo-inverse be \emph{chosen}, one for each null vector, respecting the symmetries of the original algebra in the sense of Definition \claimref{obj.transport.equivariance}? The natural conjecture, and the founding conjecture of this programme, asserts that it can, one ascent up:
__notes__.note.transport.hyperbolic-atom:
The assumption $n \geq 3$ is necessary, and the bound is sharp. For $n = 2$ the space is itself a hyperbolic plane, $U = 0$, there are no null rotations, and the assignment $\sigma(\lambda v) = \lambda^{-1} w_0$, $\sigma(\lambda w_0) = \lambda^{-1} v$ defines a genuinely $\Pin(1,1)$-equivariant pseudo-inverse section in the sense of Definition \claimref{obj.transport.equivariance}, and no ascent is needed: the hyperbolic plane is self-complete \emph{at the level of elements}. (Its reciprocal on \emph{points} is of course still partial; Theorem \claimref{transport.totality} applies to it like any other base, and its own transport is $\Cl(2,2)$. The two senses of completion are exactly the two halves of the transport principle, and the atom separates them.)

The section has a coordinate-free description, which is the real reason for its equivariance and simultaneously explains the failure for $n \geq 3$. For null $x$, call $y$ a \emph{partner} of $x$ if $y$ is null with $x \cdot y = \tfrac12$. Writing $y = av + bw_0 + u$ with $u \in U$, the two conditions read $b = 1$ and $a = -Q(u)$, so the partners of $v$ are exactly
\begin{equation}
y_u \;=\; w_0 - u - Q(u)\,v \qquad (u \in U),
\end{equation}
an affine space of dimension $n - 2$ on which, by Step 2 of Theorem \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements}, the null rotations act simply transitively. For $n = 2$ it is a single point, so ``the partner of $x$'' is a well-formed metric description and $\sigma$ is equivariant for that reason alone, with no computation; for $n \geq 3$ a torsor has no distinguished point, and Theorem \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements} says no enlargement of the space produces one. This is precisely why the hyperbolic plane is the unit of transport: the ascent of the section “The completion: the conformal model” adjoins a copy of the one quadratic space that needs no ascent of the first kind.


The same dimension count is Zeeman's. By Zeeman's theorem \cite{Zeeman1964}, for $n \geq 3$ every bijection of Minkowski space preserving the causal order is generated by Lorentz transformations, translations and dilations, while in $n = 2$ the two null coordinates can be reparametrised independently and the causal automorphism group is infinite-dimensional. The two-dimensional counterexamples to Zeeman are exactly the freedom that the null rotations remove for $n \geq 3$ by mixing each null direction with the transverse ones; the little group of a null direction has a null-rotation part of dimension $n - 2$, and both theorems hold precisely when it is present. Zeeman's theorem is imported here, not proved, and nothing below depends on it; this paragraph records that the third hypothesis of Theorem \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements} and Zeeman's are the same hypothesis, the existence of a null rotation, so that the hyperbolic atom is the exception to both for one reason.
__notes__.note.singularity.setting-introduction:
The information paradox is usually posed as a conflict between two theories. This paper poses it as a comparison of entropies computed in two algebras, and computes them.

The setting is gauge theory gravity (GTG), the formulation of general relativity in the spacetime algebra $\Cl(1,3)$ due to Lasenby, Doran and Gull \cite{LDG1998}, in which gravity is a gauge field $\hb$, a position-dependent linear map on vectors, and every metrical statement is built from $\hb^{-1}$: the theory's geometric content exists exactly where $\hb$ is invertible. the section “Step 1: locate the failure” sets the theory out exactly, field equations, connection bivector and gauge laws included, because the chain's first step is a statement about those equations and must be made in them. For Schwarzschild in the Newtonian gauge, $\hb$ is invertible in closed form at every $r > 0$, horizon included, and is unimodular there, so nothing determinant-like ever degenerates: the divergence is carried entirely by the connection bivector, and at $r = 0$ the description fails in every gauge, through a null kernel, in the exact rescaled-limit sense of Proposition \claimref{singularity.degeneration-exactly}. The singularity is a division-by-zero locus in the literal, algebraic sense, and the transport principle of this series, the root paper T1 \cite{ButlerT1}, is a general theory of exactly such loci: it classifies the obstruction, forces a minimal completion, and quantifies what any return to the original level must lose. Its operational form is the six-step transport algorithm of \cite[\S 8.1, Table 1]{ButlerT1}, and this paper is that algorithm run end to end on the black hole; the table accompanying \claimref{singularity.imported-equivalence-einstein-equations} gives the step-by-step correspondence.

The paper runs the resulting chain from the classical field to the Page curve, numbered by the transport algorithm of the root paper with the physics expanded where it lies (Steps 1 to 3, 4a to 4e, 5, 6a and 6b), each step carrying its declared status (proved, or proved from named premises). The steps are summarised in the table accompanying \claimref{singularity.imported-equivalence-einstein-equations} and constitute the paper's outline. Steps 1 through 5 are theorems, at their stated scopes: the location and type of the failure, the forced ascent to $\Cl(2,4)$, the installation of canonical anticommutation relations where classical repair is barred, on the approach by Fact \claimref{singularity.imported-no-c-number-repair} and at the boundary itself by Fact \claimref{singularity.imported-no-equivariant-value-wall}, the selection of the boost plane and its rate, the identity of boost and number operator, single-mode thermality at exactly $\TH$ with the state's marginals fixed by univalence and one regularity premise rather than assumed, the bosonic Planck sector by bosonisation in the s-wave-reduced sector under the named joint quasi-freeness premise (Q), and the lossy descent with its exact multi-mode cost (Theorem \claimref{singularity.deficit-theorem-cost-descent-exactly}). Steps 6a and 6b remain conditional in substance, but every condition is a \emph{named postulate}: the boundary-mode capacity is a theorem from three axioms (curvature cutoff, cell density, counted epoch, the causal-epoch integral computed exactly in Lemma \claimref{singularity.causal-epoch-computed-exactly}), the radiation entropy of the rate model is an exact identity from localisation, purity, capacity, injection and boundary-mode locality, with the Page envelope its corollary and exact saturation confined to the zero-frequency idealisation, of which the linear weights supply exactly one mode, the sea level, so no window of two or more members ever saturates, the no-attic condition is derived rather than assumed, and the envelope with its endpoint needs no typicality and no assumption about where correlations are placed, boundary-mode locality being the one dynamical premise. The chain's conclusion on the paradox is a dissolution rather than a resolution: information is lost at the $\Cl(1,3)$ level and preserved at the $\Cl(2,4)$ level, these are the same physics read at two levels, and the discrepancy between the levels is not destruction but a fixed algebraic projection whose thermal output is the Hawking flux itself and whose size is an equation: the relative entropy of Theorem \claimref{singularity.deficit-theorem-cost-descent-exactly}, carried entirely by the correlations of the quanta (Corollary \claimref{singularity.deficit-carried-quanta-correlations}).

The paper also contains an exactly solvable finite-mode model (the section “The finite-mode model: the dissolution step by step”) in which the dissolution can be followed step by step, at both levels. In the model, every single radiated quantum is \emph{provably, exactly} thermal, by a parity-protection lemma stating that no encoding by phase scrambling can be visible to any single-quantum measurement; the joint radiation state is pure; the information is recoverable from inter-quanta correlations; the mutual-information computation per emission, together with the Page-shaped entropy sequence, is computed in exact arithmetic and machine-verified; and the multi-mode descent is applied to the radiation outright (the section “The descent, applied: the two levels in numbers”), so that the two-level conclusion is exhibited in exact numbers (the table accompanying \claimref{singularity.purity-correlation-transfer-recovery} and Proposition \claimref{singularity.two-levels-finite-model}) rather than argued. The model is a toy by construction and is offered as one: its value is that every claim in it is a computation, so the chain's conceptual endpoint (thermality as the record of what the projection cannot see; correlations as its carrier) is exhibited rather than argued.

A word on the standard of proof, binding throughout. The environments Theorem, Proposition and Lemma, with a Proof, are reserved for results proved \emph{in this paper}, at the standard of T1 \cite{ButlerT1}. Results proved elsewhere that the chain needs are stated as \textbf{Facts (imported)}, with their precise provenance; the typography tracks the epistemic content, so a reader can see at a glance which links of the chain this paper carries and which it inherits. Four links not previously proved are proved here outright: the finite-dimensional modular theory behind Step 4d; the state selection that completes it, the identification of the descent with the fermion parity average and the rigidity theorem that follows (Theorems \claimref{singularity.descent-parity-average}, \claimref{singularity.ascended-marginals-are-diagonal}, \claimref{singularity.rate-rigidity-temperature-not-algebra-intrinsic}); the curvature behind Step 4b, derived in the gauge formalism in the text (Theorem \claimref{singularity.curvature-gauge-field-exact-shape-decoupling}), with the appendix as an independent metric-picture cross-check; and the multi-mode descent behind Steps 5 and 6b, with its deficit theorem (Theorem \claimref{singularity.deficit-theorem-cost-descent-exactly}).

Throughout, the physics the chain touches is kept in the text deliberately: $\Cl(2,4)$ as the conformal algebra and the twistor connection (Step 3), Israel's thermofield double and the Bisognano-Wichmann-Sewell mechanism (Step 4d), the island dictionary and the Hayden-Preskill mirror (Step 6b). These points of contact frame what kind of object the chain produces at each stage; the derivations do not depend on them.

__notes__.note.singularity.what-instance-shows-wha: The computation is the algorithm's own diagnosis, made concrete: in the completion the division never fails, and what fails is the return to the original space. The answer to ``divide by the dying direction'' exists as a point of $\mathcal{Q}_p$ and is not a vector of spacetime, so no assignment of a classical partner value can be read off it. That is the point-level counterpart of the element-level no-go recorded next as Fact \claimref{singularity.imported-no-c-number-repair}, and the two together are what force the repair to be delivered as operators: the value has left the space, and the algebra keeps only the ladder pair $v^2 = (v^*)^2 = 0, \qquad v v^* + v^* v = 1$ that records it.
__notes__.note.singularity.setting-point-level-tra: What Rule 1 installs instead of a value is the pair $v^2 = (v^*)^2 = 0, \qquad v v^* + v^* v = 1$ itself: the canonical anticommutation relations of one fermionic mode. Nothing commuting satisfies these relations; objects obeying them are irreducibly operators on a two-state space. By the localisation of \cite[Cor.~4.5]{ButlerT4}, in the form the Schwarzschild composite gives it at the black hole \cite[Thm.~8.12]{ButlerT4} (reproduced verbatim, hypotheses included, as Facts \claimref{sheaf.schwarzschild-degeneration-boundary-tame} and \claimref{singularity.imported-one-sided-completion-singularity} in the section “The imported localisation theorems, verbatim”), exactly one such mode is at each point of the blown-up singular locus $E \cong \R \times S^2$, and nowhere else in the physical closure: the composite's corank-one theorem \cite[Thm.~8.7]{ButlerT4} makes the count one pair per point, not one per dying coordinate direction. Quantisation is demanded locally, exactly where the classical description divides by zero, and is output rather than input: no quantisation procedure is imposed anywhere; the strength of ``demanded'' is uniform: barred on the approach by Fact \claimref{singularity.imported-no-c-number-repair} and at the boundary itself by Fact \claimref{singularity.imported-no-equivariant-value-wall}.
__notes__.note.singularity.setting-step-3-apply-ru: \emph{Where the ascent lands.} $\Cl(2,4)$ is not an anonymous algebra. It is the conformal geometric algebra of Minkowski space, obtained by adjoining the null pair $(\nO, \nInf)$ to the spacetime algebra; it is the algebra of the conformal group $\mathrm{SO}(2,4)$ of compactified Minkowski space; the spinor module of its even part is $\C^4$, Penrose's twistor space \cite{Penrose1967}; and $\mathrm{SO}(2,4)$ is the isometry group underlying $\mathrm{AdS}_5$, hence the symmetry algebra of the best-studied holographic correspondence. The mechanical rule, applied to the unique locus in classical physics where division by zero is unavoidable, selects the algebra Penrose has argued for five decades is the correct language for precisely this regime. There is independent physical evidence pointing the same way: near a generic singularity every mass scale becomes negligible against the curvature scale and the dynamics is asymptotically conformally invariant, the essential observation of BKL analysis and of conformal cyclic cosmology. The metric degenerates at $r = 0$; the light cones survive; and $\Cl(2,4)$ is the light cones' algebra.
__notes__.note.singularity.three-wrinkles-recorded: First, statistics: the chain's pairs are fermionic, so the directly produced spectrum is Fermi-Dirac, correct for the fermionic sector of Hawking emission; the bosonic Planck sector is Step 4e's task and is derived, not assumed. Second, coherence with the count: at $\omega \sim \TH$ the thermal entropy per fermionic mode is of order $\ln 2$, one bit, exactly the per-mode capacity that converts Step 6a's mode count $N_{\mathrm{6a}}$ into the boundary-mode capacity $C = N_{\mathrm{6a}}\ln 2$ of Proposition \claimref{singularity.area-law-test}: the thermodynamics and the counting cohere. Third, the role of the hyperbolic atom is now complete: $\Cl(1,1)$, the unique self-complete unit of transport (Lemma \claimref{singularity.pseudo-inverse-identities-hyperbolic-atom}), is the horizon's boost plane, matched to the curvature-selected plane by Corollary \claimref{singularity.matching-steps-4b-4c-join-equation}, and its intrinsic structure, the unique rotor flow with its spectral projectors, is the modular structure of black hole thermodynamics. The atom that needs no ascent is the one that carries the temperature.

__notes__.note.transport.setting-transport-princip:
The Principle is a summary, not an axiom: each of its clauses is one of the theorems proved above, and it adds nothing to them. What it does add is the reading. The three costs are not a graded scale of difficulty but three different answers to one equivariance question, and the question is answerable at all only because the taxonomy is exhaustive: it is the completeness of Theorem \claimref{transport.exhaustiveness-every-zero-divisor-annihilated-idempotent}, not the ingenuity of any rule, that turns a family of repairs into a procedure.

Two closing observations. First, the shape of the type-N answer is the surprising one, and it is worth stating plainly that it is a change of level rather than a technical fix: what is repaired is not the element, which remains non-invertible in every enlargement however large, but the space in which the element's division was asked. Second, no transport removes all obstructions. Every completion carries obstructions of its own, and in the type-N case the adjoined pair is itself null (Proposition \claimref{transport.no-transport-terminates}): the repair of the old null cone is effected by adjoining new members of it. What the bookkeeping of the section “The mod-8 clock and the one-way door” shows is therefore not that transport terminates but that it stabilises, the clock moving at most once and then remaining fixed. Obstruction is conserved; what the rules achieve is that it no longer changes the Wedderburn type.

The paper is intended to be independently checkable throughout: every algebraic statement can be verified from the axiom $v^2 = Q(v)$ with pencil and paper, the topological statements of the section “Totality of the transported reciprocal” from the elementary point-set facts recorded in the section “The completion: the conformal model”, and every computational identity by the deposited scripts.

__notes__.note.transport.moore-penrose-boundary-id: One refinement of the type-P question does carry content, and it traces the boundary of the section “The hyperbolic atom as a matrix algebra: the Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse” from the other side. Within the idempotents sharing a fixed image $W$, is there a canonical one? They are in bijection with the complements of $W$, hence form a torsor under $\mathrm{Hom}(V/W, W)$ on which the stabiliser of $W$ acts by unipotent transvections, the same shear mechanism as the null rotations of Lemma \claimref{transport.group-null-rotations}. For type P the ambiguity concerns only \emph{which} idempotent to use, and the repair theorem needs no choice at all, since $\sigma(e) = e$ is asked about a given $e$; for type N the same ambiguity affects the repair itself, which is why the null cone needs the ascent and the idempotent variety does not.
__notes__.note.transport.setting-introduction:
In ordinary arithmetic, division fails at exactly one number, and the failure is handled by prohibition: division by zero is forbidden, and every calculation routes around it. This paper is about the same failure in a richer setting. A Clifford algebra is the algebra of a geometry: its elements are built from the vectors of a space, and its one rule is that a vector times itself is its squared length. In such an algebra most elements can be divided by. Every vector of nonzero length has an exact inverse, and these invertible elements are plentiful enough to build every symmetry of the underlying space \cite{HestenesSobczyk1984, DoranLasenby2003}. But with three exceptions (the real numbers, the complex numbers and the quaternions, the three Clifford algebras that are themselves division algebras), every real Clifford algebra also contains nonzero elements that cannot be inverted at all: elements that multiply with some partner to give exactly zero, the \emph{zero divisors}. Where they occur, division fails, and the standard response is arithmetic's response: exclude them and work around the exclusion.

The response examined here is the opposite one, and it is the founding idea of the programme this paper begins: read each failure of division as an instruction. A failure, precisely located, tells you what the algebra is missing. The theorems of this paper show that it also tells you the smallest thing that can be added to supply it, and that the addition is forced, not chosen.

The stance has a precedent in the foundations of mathematics, and the precedent was in fact the founding idea's model. G\"odel proved that any consistent system strong enough for arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove. The famous part is the impossibility; the instructive part is its precision. The unprovable statement is informative: it names, exactly, the stronger system in which it becomes a theorem, and that stronger system contains new unprovable statements of its own, without end. This paper proves that division by zero in a Clifford algebra has the same structure. The impossibility is internal and exact: an inverse of a null vector $v$ would satisfy $vv^{-1} = 1$, and multiplying by $v$ reduces it to $v = 0$ (Lemma \claimref{transport.noinverse}). The failure determines its own repair, exactly one hyperbolic plane, which is the minimality half of the type-N theorems. And the completed algebra carries a new null cone of its own, so the ascent never terminates; the resulting tower is the subject of T3 \cite{ButlerT3}. The parallel is structural, not a theorem, since provability and invertibility belong to different categories, and nothing below depends on it. What it supplies is the right way to read what follows: the limit of a system indicates the system that removes it, and mathematics has met this kind of obstruction before.

The failures come in exactly three kinds, each with a concrete description. A \emph{null vector} is a direction whose squared length is zero; in spacetime these are the directions light travels, and no algebra containing such a vector can invert it. An \emph{idempotent} is an element with $e^2 = e$, one of the algebra's projections; every projection other than $0$ and $1$ annihilates its complementary projection, so each is a zero divisor. And in certain signatures the algebra splits into two independent halves that annihilate each other; the \emph{central} idempotents that effect this split are the deepest failure of the three, because no symmetry of the algebra can even exchange the halves. We prove this list complete: every zero divisor belongs to one of the three kinds. For each kind the paper then proves the repair. The null vector cannot be repaired as an element: once the space has more than two dimensions, no assignment of pseudo-inverses (the standard weakened substitute for an inverse, recalled in the section “Setting, and the classical facts the proofs use”) can respect the symmetries of the space, whether valued in the algebra itself, in the Clifford algebra of any extension of the space, or in a matrix algebra over one (the scope of Theorem \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements} and Remark \claimref{note.transport.obstruction-parabolic}); the two-dimensional hyperbolic plane is the only exception, and an instructive one. What can be repaired is the space of points itself, by a completion that costs exactly one new plane and makes the reciprocal total; no smaller completion works. The split algebra is repaired by one added generator, which fuses its two halves into a single simple algebra, again minimally. The ordinary projection turns out to need no repair at all: it is its own pseudo-inverse. And the repairs compose cleanly, so a repair never creates a failure it cannot finish.

The plan of the paper is the plan just sketched, now with theorems attached. First classify: the three kinds have sharp existence loci, and the classification is exhaustive (the section “A taxonomy of obstructions”). Then repair, one kind per section. \emph{Isotropic vectors} exist precisely in mixed signature; they are the most geometric of the obstructions and the only genuinely hard one, and their treatment takes the longest section of the paper (the section “Type N: the isotropic obstruction, and Rule 1”). \emph{Central idempotents} exist precisely in the split signatures $p - q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, where the algebra splits into two ideals that no inner symmetry can exchange, and where, on the one-dimensional extensions of the even-dimensional algebras, the repair turns out to coincide with the first rule's ascent (the section “Type C: ideal fusion, and Rule 2”). \emph{Non-central idempotents} exist everywhere else, and demand nothing at all (the section “Type P: the rule of no rule”). Each repair comes with the theorem that makes it forced rather than convenient, the bookkeeping of iterated repairs is settled in the section “The mod-8 clock and the one-way door”, and the section “The transport principle, and the algorithm” states what it all amounts to: a general principle, and a six-step procedure whose every step is licensed by a theorem proved earlier in the paper. the table accompanying \claimref{transport.transport-algorithm} there is the paper's contribution list in operational form.

__notes__.note.transport.locality-robustness-obstr:
The proof consumes far less than the theorem's hypotheses offer, and it is worth recording what it actually uses, since the surplus rules out the obvious weakenings.

\emph{It is local.} Only the stabiliser of a \emph{single} null vector enters. The sharp statement proved above is therefore: \emph{for one null vector $v$ there is no $\sigma \in \Cl(\mathbb{V}')$ with $v\sigma v = v$ that is invariant under the null rotations fixing $v$.} No global rule, no coherence across the cone, and no regularity of $\sigma$ (continuity, measurability, genericity) is assumed or would help; the theorem as stated follows at once.

\emph{It survives equivariance up to scale.} The natural first weakening is to ask only that $\sigma(v)$ be canonical projectively, $\tau_R(\sigma(v)) = \lambda\,\sigma(v)$ for some $\lambda \neq 0$. This fails too. In the normal form of Step 1 the $w_0$-coefficient is $\gamma = 1$, and Step 3 shows it is unchanged by conjugation; comparing $w_0$-components forces $\lambda = 1$, whereupon the $\Cl(U')$-comparison gives the same contradiction $u = 0$.
__notes__.note.transport.obstruction-parabolic: The stabiliser of a null direction in an indefinite orthogonal group is not \emph{reductive}: it contains a nontrivial normal subgroup of \emph{unipotent} elements, transformations $g$ for which $g - \mathrm{id}$ is nilpotent (here $(R-1)^2 = 0$ in the algebra, while on $\mathbb{V}$ the action satisfies $(\Ad_R - \mathrm{id})^3 = 0$, with $(\Ad_R - \mathrm{id})^2 w_0 = -2Q(u)\,v$ nonzero whenever $Q(u) \neq 0$), called its unipotent radical. (``Parabolic'' parallels the M\"obius classification: like a parabolic M\"obius map, a null rotation is unipotent and fixes the null direction $[v]$; for $n = 3$ it fixes no other direction at all, while for $n \geq 4$ it fixes in addition the subspace $U \cap u^{\perp}$, which may itself contain null directions.) Step 3 shows that this radical acts on the candidate partners by translating the $\Cl(U')$-coefficient $\alpha$ by $-u$, freely and without fixed point; Proposition \claimref{transport.pseudo-inverse-torsor} makes that action exact. Two consequences deserve emphasis. First, enlarging the algebra can never help: the shearing rotors $R = 1 + vu$ and the translation vectors $u$ lie inside $\Cl(\mathbb{V})$ and act the same way in every extension, which is why Theorem \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements} quantifies over all ascents at once. The quantifier ranges over the Clifford algebra of an extension quadratic space (Definition \claimref{obj.transport.extension-quadratic-spaces}), which is what the splitting of Lemma \claimref{transport.splitting-along-hyperbolic-plane} requires; it extends verbatim to matrix algebras $M_k\bigl(\Cl(\mathbb{V}')\bigr)$ over such an algebra, since reading $v\sigma v = v$ entrywise, with $v$ embedded as $v\,I$, makes each diagonal entry of $\sigma$ an invariant pseudo-inverse in $\Cl(\mathbb{V}')$ and so contradicts the theorem. Second, the phenomenon is absent in definite signature, where there are no null vectors and stabilisers of directions are compact and reductive: it is a genuinely mixed-signature obstruction, present exactly where the null cone is.

__notes__.note.transport.setting-euclidean-plane-i:
Take the base $\mathbb{V} = \R^2$ with $Q$ positive definite (signature $(2,0)$), and identify $\mathbb{V}$ with $\C$ by $z = x + iy$, so that $Q(z) = |z|^2$. Definite signature has no null vectors, so the partial locus of $\rho(z) = z/Q(z)$ is the origin alone: this is the oldest division by zero there is. Note which hypotheses are at work. The no-go theorem requires $p, q \geq 1$ and $n \geq 3$ and does not apply here, since with no null vectors there is no element-level question to obstruct, while the theorems this example exercises (totality, minimality, the normal form) hold in every nondegenerate signature, as recorded in the scope paragraph of the section “Quadratic spaces and Clifford algebras”.

The completion is $\Cl(3,1)$. Because $Q$ is definite, the incidence condition \claimref{transport.swap-rescale-normal-form} with $s = 0$ forces $z = 0$: the ideal strata (i) and (ii) of Proposition \claimref{transport.swap-rescale-normal-form} are empty, and the only ideal point is $[\nInf]$, stratum (iii). The quadric $\mathcal{Q}$ is therefore the plane with a single point adjoined, and the map
\[
[X(z)] \;\mapsto\; \frac{1}{|z|^2+1}\bigl(\,2x,\; 2y,\; |z|^2 - 1\,\bigr), \qquad [\nInf] \;\mapsto\; (0,0,1)
\]
identifies $\mathcal{Q}$ with the unit sphere $S^2 \subset \R^3$ by inverse stereographic projection from the north pole. This is the Riemann sphere, with $[X(0)]$ the south pole and $[\nInf]$ the point at infinity.

Under this identification, Theorem \claimref{transport.totality} computes
\[
\iota[X(z)] = [X(z/|z|^2)] \ \ (z \neq 0), \qquad \iota[X(0)] = [\nInf], \qquad \iota[\nInf] = [X(0)],
\]
and $z \mapsto z/|z|^2 = 1/\bar{z}$ is inversion in the unit circle. On the sphere it is the reflection
\[
(X, Y, Z) \;\mapsto\; (X, Y, -Z)
\]
in the equatorial plane: the modulus inverts and the argument is unchanged, so the equator $|z| = 1$ is fixed pointwise and the two poles, $0$ and $\infty$, are exchanged. Both statements are Proposition \claimref{transport.swap-rescale-normal-form} read in these coordinates, the second being the fixed locus $\{Q = 1\} \cup \text{(ii)}$ of Remark \claimref{note.transport.where-each-stratum-comes} with the stratum (ii) that definite signature leaves empty. Inversion in a circle is anti-holomorphic; the holomorphic $z \mapsto 1/z$ of complex analysis is its composite with the reflection $y \mapsto -y$, which is a reflection of the base and so a versor of the model. Either way the content tested is the same, and it is the classical one: a reciprocal undefined at a single point of the plane becomes a total involution of a compact surface two dimensions up, with $1/0 = \infty$ and $1/\infty = 0$. Theorem \claimref{transport.totality} reproduces the nineteenth-century resolution of $1/0$ by conformal compactification, as it must, and Theorem \claimref{transport.minimality} adds that the two dimensions it uses are the fewest that will serve.

The same computation over the one-dimensional base $\mathbb{V} = \R$, $Q(x) = x^2$, has completion $\Cl(2,1)$, identifies $\mathcal{Q}$ with the real projective line $\R P^1$ in its classical homogeneous coordinates $[\,x : s\,]$, and returns for $\iota$ the classical inversion matrix $\begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}$, with $[\,0:1\,]$ and $[\,1:0\,]$ exchanged.

What no definite signature exhibits, in either dimension, is the null cone. The genuinely new content of Theorems \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements} and \claimref{transport.totality}(3) lies on the ideal strata (i) and (ii), which are empty here and carry, in mixed signature, one class per null vector and one per null direction respectively. There the compactification adjoins a stratum rather than a point, and the element-level question is both posed and closed.
__notes__.note.transport.setting-hyperbolic-atom-m:
The algebra $\Cl(1,1)$ is isomorphic to the algebra $M_2(\R)$ of real $2 \times 2$ matrices: with $e_0^2 = 1$, $e_1^2 = -1$, the assignment
\[
e_0 \mapsto E = \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}, \qquad
e_1 \mapsto F = \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}
\]
satisfies $E^2 = I$, $F^2 = -I$ and $EF + FE = 0$, hence extends to an algebra isomorphism (both algebras have dimension four; $M_2(\R)$ is simple). A base vector $x e_0 + y e_1$ maps to $\begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & x+y \\ x-y & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}$, of determinant $-(x^2 - y^2) = -Q$: \emph{a vector is null exactly when its matrix is singular}. In particular the hyperbolic pair $v = \tfrac12(e_0 + e_1)$, $w_0 = \tfrac12(e_0 - e_1)$ (so $v \cdot w_0 = \tfrac12$) maps to
\[
v \;\mapsto\; N = \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}, \qquad
w_0 \;\mapsto\; N^{\mathsf T} = \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}.
\]
Under this dictionary the objects of the section “The refuted conjecture, and the no-go” become textbook objects of linear algebra: the equation $v\,\sigma(v)\,v = v$ is Penrose's first equation $AXA = A$ for a \emph{generalized inverse} of a singular matrix, and the abundance of pseudo-inverses noted there is the familiar abundance of generalized inverses.

Matrix theory has a canonical selection among them: the Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse $A^{+}$, which for a rank-one matrix is $A^{+} = A^{\mathsf T}/\lVert A \rVert_F^{\,2}$. Applied to the null vectors of this base,
\[
(\lambda N)^{+} = \lambda^{-1} N^{\mathsf T}, \qquad (\lambda N^{\mathsf T})^{+} = \lambda^{-1} N,
\]
which is, under the isomorphism, \emph{exactly} the equivariant section $\sigma(\lambda v) = \lambda^{-1} w_0$, $\sigma(\lambda w_0) = \lambda^{-1} v$ of Remark \claimref{note.transport.hyperbolic-atom}: the hyperbolic atom's self-completeness is the Moore--Penrose construction expressed in the Clifford algebra. The agreement is not a coincidence of formulas. By \claimref{note.transport.hyperbolic-atom} the partner of a null vector in a hyperbolic plane is unique, so any rule at all that returns a null partner returns this one; the Euclidean transpose supplies it, and so does the metric description.

The agreement extends to the failure, which is the instructive part. It is classical that $A^{+}$ is canonical only relative to a choice of \emph{definite} inner product: it is built from the transpose, the adjoint of the Euclidean metric, and transforms correctly under orthogonal maps, $(UAV)^{+} = V^{\mathsf T} A^{+}\, U^{\mathsf T}$ for orthogonal $U, V$, but not under general invertible ones. Known theory therefore already signals that the obvious candidate for $\sigma$ must fail to respect an \emph{indefinite} symmetry group, which preserves no definite inner product. Theorem \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements} is the sharp form of that signal. For $n = 2$ the stabiliser of a null direction in $O(1,1)$ contains no null rotations, nothing shears, the partner set \claimref{note.transport.hyperbolic-atom} is a single point, and the Moore--Penrose choice survives as an equivariant section (Remark \claimref{note.transport.hyperbolic-atom}). For $n \geq 3$ the stabiliser acquires a unipotent radical of null rotations, the partner set becomes a torsor under it, and not only the Moore--Penrose rule but \emph{every conceivable rule}, valued in the Clifford algebra of any extension or in a matrix algebra over it, is sheared away. The no-go theorem thus marks the precise boundary of the Moore--Penrose phenomenon: canonical generalized inversion of null directions ends exactly where parabolic stabilisers begin.
__notes__.note.transport.why-shear-has-nothing-act: The proposition looks too easy to be the analogue of Theorem \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements}, so it is worth locating exactly where the difficulty of type N disappears. It is not in the shear, which is present on both sides: the pseudo-inverses of a null vector form a torsor under the null rotations (Proposition \claimref{transport.pseudo-inverse-torsor}), and the idempotents sharing the image of $e$ form one under $\mathrm{Hom}$-groups that the stabiliser of $e$ shears in exactly the same unipotent manner (Remark \claimref{note.transport.moore-penrose-boundary-idempotent-side} below). The difference is what the torsor contains. The null vector is not a member of its own repair family, since $v\,v\,v = 0 \neq v$, so equivariance must select from a set with no invariant point; the idempotent is a member of its own, since $eee = e$, so the repair need not lie in the sheared directions at all. One identity separates the two cases. The taxonomy's three transport costs, namely a hyperbolic plane for N (and even then only at the level of points), one generator for C, and nothing for P, are thus not a graded scale of difficulty but three different answers to the same equivariance question, each carrying its own theorem.
__notes__.note.transport.what-procedure-does-not-d:
Three boundaries, each a theorem rather than a caution.

It never returns an inverse. For type N no element-level repair exists at all (Theorem \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements}); what the ascent supplies is a total operation on points together with a canonical destination for the values the base cannot hold. A reader who wants $1/v$ will not find it here, and Theorem \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements} is the statement that nobody will.

It assumes the form is nondegenerate. Everything above is stated for nondegenerate $(\mathbb{V},Q)$. A degenerate form is not a harder case of the same problem but a different one: its radical generates a square-zero ideal rather than a resolvable obstruction (Theorem \claimref{transport.one-generator-minimal-minimal-completions-classified}(2) is the fibre-level instance), and completing it is the subject of the series' sheaf-theoretic paper \cite{ButlerT4}.

It is a procedure for one algebra. When division fails not at a point of an algebra but along a locus of a family, the rank of the relevant bundle cannot jump, and the correct object is a pair of sheaves rather than a single ascent: the fibrewise version of Step 3, with the completion performed over the degenerate locus and only there, is \cite[Thm.\ 4.4, Cor.\ 4.5]{ButlerT4}.

__notes__.note.transport.abstract: The usual response to a zero divisor is exclusion. This paper, the root of the programme, takes the opposite: read the failure as an instruction. Division fails in a real Clifford algebra of nondegenerate form in exactly three ways: at isotropic vectors, central idempotents, and non-central idempotents. We prove the trichotomy exhaustive and, for each failure, the minimal repair and the theorem that makes it forced. From dimension three, isotropic vectors admit no equivariant repair at the level of elements, in the Clifford algebra of any extension: the null rotations shear every candidate partner, and the obstruction is a tautological cohomology class vanishing only for the hyperbolic plane. The ascent repairs instead the space of points: the reciprocal extends totally, continuously and uniquely to the null quadric of $\Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1)$, and the increment $(+1,+1)$ is forced twice over, by a sign argument on lifts and an embedding-independent rank computation. Central idempotents ascend by one generator, making the grade involution inner and fusing the two ideals into $\Mat_2(\Cl^0(p,q))$, minimal among the simple real algebras into which the split algebra embeds unitally; the sign of the adjoined direction is a bit the algebra forgets. Non-central idempotents demand nothing, because $eee = e$ where $vvv = 0$. Under iteration, Rule 1 fixes the mod-8 clock, fusion occurs at most once, and no unital homomorphism returns to the base. A closing section states the principle and a six-step algorithm. Every computational identity is machine-verified in exact rational arithmetic, except one flagged floating-point Moore--Penrose check.
__notes__.note.transport.setting-contribution:
What this paper adds is not the classification and not the conformal model, but the reading they jointly permit: the organisation of the zero divisors of $\Cl(p,q)$ into three obstruction types with sharp existence loci; the no-go theorem that closes the element-level repair of the isotropic type, with its cohomological form; the minimality theorems that make each rule forced, in a representation-independent sense; and the change of reading these mandate, namely that the conformal construction is not an available convenience but the unique minimal completion demanded by the failure of division itself.

At the standard of complete proofs, with every theorem carrying its own hypotheses and every computational identity machine-verified, the paper proves: that the zero divisors of $\Cl(p,q)$ fall into exactly three types with sharp existence loci, and that the trichotomy is exhaustive because every zero divisor is annihilated by a nontrivial idempotent (the section “A taxonomy of obstructions”); that isotropic vectors admit no equivariant element-level repair in the Clifford algebra of any extension once $n \geq 3$, the obstruction being the tautological class of the unipotent radical, whose vanishing locus is exactly the hyperbolic atom (the section “The refuted conjecture, and the no-go” and the section “The obstruction as a cohomology class”); that the reciprocal nevertheless extends totally, continuously and uniquely to the null quadric of the completion (the section “The completion: the conformal model” and the section “Totality of the transported reciprocal”); that the increment $(+1,+1)$ is forced twice over, by a sign argument on lifts and by a rank computation on ambient quadrics that no exotic embedding evades (the section “Minimality among null-lift completions” and the section “Minimality against arbitrary embeddings”); that central idempotents fuse under a one-generator ascent into $\Mat_2(\Cl^0(p,q))$, minimal among all simple real algebras, with the sign of the adjoined direction a bit the algebra forgets, and that on every one-dimensional extension of an even-dimensional algebra exactly one sign obstructs, its ideals are copies of the base, and the opposite-sign repair is the Rule 1 ascent, so that the two rules coincide there (the section “Type C: ideal fusion, and Rule 2”); that non-central idempotents demand nothing, because $eee = e$ where $vvv = 0$, so there is no fourth rule (the section “Type P: the rule of no rule”); and that the bookkeeping closes, Rule 1 fixing the mod-8 clock, fusion occurring at most once, and no unital homomorphism returning to the base (the section “The mod-8 clock and the one-way door”).
__notes__.note.transport.setting-null-vectors-zero: Division fails first, and most geometrically, at the null vectors, and the facts of this subsection are the paper's own.

Null vectors are moreover two-sided zero divisors. The obstruction they pose is packaged in the reciprocal map
\[
\rho : \mathbb{V} \setminus \{Q = 0\} \to \mathbb{V}, \qquad \rho(x) = x / Q(x),
\]
which is partial exactly on $\{Q = 0\}$, the null cone together with the origin. Both failure modes are resolved by the same completion (Theorem \claimref{transport.totality}); only the null cone poses the element-level question of the section “The refuted conjecture, and the no-go”, the pseudo-inverse condition being vacuous at the origin.

Null vectors come in pairs. If $v$ is null and $Q$ is nondegenerate, there is a vector $a$ with $v \cdot a \neq 0$; rescaling so that $v \cdot a = \tfrac12$ and setting $w = a - Q(a)\,v$ gives
\[
Q(w) = Q(a) - 2\,Q(a)\,(v \cdot a) = 0, \qquad v \cdot w = v \cdot a = \tfrac12 :
\]
a \emph{hyperbolic pair} $(v, w)$. The plane $H = \mathrm{span}\{v, w\}$ is a \emph{hyperbolic plane}: its Gram matrix on $(v,w)$ has determinant $-\tfrac14$, so $H$ is nondegenerate of signature $(1,1)$, and conversely every two-dimensional nondegenerate space containing a null vector is isometric to $H$ \cite{Lam2005}. Inside the Clifford algebra a hyperbolic pair satisfies
\begin{equation}
v^2 = w^2 = 0, \qquad vw + wv = 1, \qquad \text{hence} \quad vwv = (1 - wv)v = v .
\end{equation}
The last identity says $w$ is a \emph{pseudo-inverse} of $v$ in the sense of von Neumann: division by $v$ cannot be undone exactly, but $w$ undoes it up to the defect of $v$. This is the weakened form of inversion around which the section “The refuted conjecture, and the no-go” revolves.
__notes__.note.transport.setting-position-series:
This paper is T1 of the series.

\emph{This paper relies on:} the companion primer T0 \cite{ButlerT0}, and on nothing else in the series. The division of labour is strict: the language belongs to the primer (the structural lemmas of the section “Setting, and the classical facts the proofs use” are restated with their toolkit numbers, and proved in the primer's toolkit \cite[Section 9]{ButlerT0}, save the classification theorem, cited there to its classical sources), while every fact about the failure of division, zero divisors, pseudo-inverses and idempotents included, is stated and proved in this paper. Beyond the toolkit the primer is a convenience for readers new to geometric algebra. The paper's other input is the founding idea of the programme itself, whose informal taxonomy it rigorises.

\emph{Papers that rely on this one:} every other research paper of the series. In brief: T2 \cite{ButlerT2} takes the element-level lemma that a square-zero element is invertible in no unital extension (Lemma \claimref{transport.noinverse}), the type-N reading of a radical direction with the taxonomy frame, and the scope of the sharpenings of the section “Minimality against arbitrary embeddings”, and proves its own completion theorem for degenerate algebras against that frame; T3 \cite{ButlerT3} iterates Rule 1 into the tower, using the Morita theorem and the pinching; T4 \cite{ButlerT4} localises the taxonomy and Rule 1 over degenerate loci, using the splitting lemma and the null-generator clause of Theorem \claimref{transport.one-generator-minimal-minimal-completions-classified}; T5 \cite{ButlerT5} runs the whole algorithm on the black-hole singularity, importing the no-go, totality, minimality, the type-C exclusion for $\Cl(1,3)$, the pinching, and the one-way door; and the papers after T5 \cite{ButlerT5} import these results through T3 \cite{ButlerT3}, T4 \cite{ButlerT4} and T5 \cite{ButlerT5} rather than directly, with each paper's Fact environments carrying the exact provenance. One subsection points forward without relying on anything: the sentence after Corollary \claimref{transport.which-residues-obstruct-which-way} names the dark-matter paper T14 \cite{ButlerT14} for the residues $\{2, 6\}$. __notes__.note.transport.cl-1-1-n-p-together: $v = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(e_1 + e_2)$, $w = \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}(e_1 - e_2)$ form a hyperbolic pair; $e = wv = \tfrac12(1 + e_1e_2)$ is the annihilating idempotent of Example \claimref{note.transport.hyperbolic-partner-supplies-annihilating-idempotent}, non-central; the algebra is $\Mat_2(\R)$ ($d = 0$), simple, and every zero divisor is N/P. This is the hyperbolic atom of Remark \claimref{note.transport.hyperbolic-atom} below, the one mixed signature where the element-level choice of $w$ is canonical.
__notes__.note.transport.cl-1-0-cl-2-1: $\Cl(1,0) \cong \R \oplus \R$ ($d = 1$): $\omega = e_1$, $\omega^2 = +1$, central; $\varepsilon_\pm = \tfrac12(1 \pm e_1)$; the only zero divisors are the multiples of $\varepsilon_\pm$: type C in its purest form, with no N (definite) and no P (division-algebra summands). $\Cl(2,1)$ ($d = 1$, dimension 8) $\cong \Mat_2(\R) \oplus \Mat_2(\R)$: the algebra of $2{+}1$-dimensional spacetime carries all three types at once: null vectors (mixed signature), matrix idempotents in each ideal, and the central pair $\tfrac12(1 \pm e_1e_2e_3)$.
__notes__.note.transport.cl-1-3-physical-case-n: $d = -2 \equiv 6$: $\Cl(1,3) \cong \Mat_2(\HH)$ is simple: no type C, which is what the singularity paper's diagnosis requires: there the black-hole obstruction is type N and Rule 1 (the $(1,1)$ ascent to $\Cl(2,4)$) is the operative rule.
__notes__.note.transport.setting-type-n-isotropic-: This is the hard case, and it takes the longest section of the paper. The plan: first the question, can the non-invertible element itself be repaired in the next ascent, and the theorem that closes it, with its cohomological sharpening (the section “The refuted conjecture, and the no-go”, the section “The obstruction as a cohomology class”); then the completion in which the repair succeeds at the level of points, and the totality theorem (the section “The completion: the conformal model”, the section “Totality of the transported reciprocal”); then the two minimality theorems that make the completion forced (the section “Minimality among null-lift completions”, the section “Minimality against arbitrary embeddings”); then the coordinate normal form and the cost of descent (the section “Coordinate normal form, and descent”); and finally two consistency checks against classical mathematics (the section “Consistency checks against known theory”).
__notes__.note.transport.setting-prior-art:
Two bodies of classical material are used, and neither is claimed.

The structure theory of the real Clifford algebras (the isomorphisms $\Cl(p,q) \cong \Mat_k(\mathbb{F})$ or $\Mat_k(\mathbb{F}) \oplus \Mat_k(\mathbb{F})$ with $\mathbb{F} \in \{\R, \C, \HH\}$ determined by $p - q$ mod $8$) goes back to Cartan and to the modern treatments of Atiyah, Bott and Shapiro \cite{ABS1964}, Porteous \cite{Porteous1995} and Lounesto \cite{Lounesto2001}; the quadratic-form background is in Lam \cite{Lam2005} and Chevalley \cite{Chevalley1997}. The computation of the centre and of the sign of $\omega^2$ (Lemmas \claimref{transport.centre} and \claimref{transport.sign}) is folklore, restated here and proved in the primer's toolkit \cite[Section 9]{ButlerT0} because the type-C theorem rests on it. Von Neumann regularity of semisimple rings, on which the exhaustiveness theorem rests, is von Neumann's \cite{vonNeumann1936}; the observation that regularity localises zero divisors at idempotents (Lemma \claimref{transport.regularity-localises-zero-divisors-idempotents}) is elementary and surely known, though we have not found it stated in the Clifford literature in the form used here. The idempotent structure of Clifford algebras is surveyed by Lounesto \cite{Lounesto2001} and, computationally, by Ab{\l}amowicz \cite{Ablamowicz1998}.

The point-level machinery of the type-N section is the \emph{conformal model} of geometric algebra and is thoroughly established. The representation of the points of a quadratic space as null rays in a space two dimensions larger, via the embedding $X(x) = \nO + x + \tfrac12 Q(x)\nInf$, together with the realisation of conformal transformations, inversions included, as versors of $\Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1)$, originates in the program of Hestenes and coworkers \cite{Hestenes2001, HLR2001}, has antecedents in the classical projective-quadric (M\"obius and Lie sphere) constructions of the nineteenth century, was given a comprehensive computational treatment by Dorst, Fontijne and Mann \cite{DFM2007}, is standard in the physics literature through Doran and Lasenby \cite{DoranLasenby2003}, and underlies the algebraic theory of conformal groups via Clifford algebras developed by Angl\`es \cite{Angles2008}. Nothing in the section “Setting, and the classical facts the proofs use” and the section “The completion: the conformal model” is claimed as new. The reader familiar with conformal geometric algebra may skim them for notation; the reader \emph{new} to geometric algebra should begin with the companion primer \cite{ButlerT0}, which develops all of this slowly and with worked examples.
__notes__.note.transport.setting-classification-ce: Finally, the regularity input. A ring is \emph{von Neumann regular} if for every $a$ there is an $x$ with $axa = a$ \cite{vonNeumann1936}.
__notes__.note.transport.setting-setting-classical: This section fixes notation and assembles the facts the proofs use, under a strict division of labour with the companion primer \cite{ButlerT0}. The \emph{language} belongs to the primer: the geometric product, blades, involutions, versors and the groups they generate, the classification, and the structural lemmas about them, which are restated below with their proofs imported from the primer's toolkit \cite[Section 9]{ButlerT0}, each statement carrying its number there (the classification theorem alone is not reproved in the toolkit, which states it and cites the classical sources for its induction). The \emph{failure of division} belongs to this paper: every fact about zero divisors, null vectors as obstructions, pseudo-inverses and idempotents is stated and proved here, because that failure is the paper's subject; the one deliberate exception is the splitting lemma (Lemma \claimref{transport.splitting-along-hyperbolic-plane}), a basis fact about hyperbolic planes rather than about failure, whose proof stays in the toolkit. The definitions specific to this paper (extension, equivariance) are likewise stated here and belong to this paper.
__notes__.note.transport.setting-quadratic-spaces-:
$(\mathbb{V}, Q)$ is a finite-dimensional real quadratic space with polarisation $a \cdot b = \tfrac12(Q(a+b) - Q(a) - Q(b))$, so $a \cdot a = Q(a)$, and is \emph{nondegenerate} when $a \cdot b = 0$ for all $b$ forces $a = 0$. It then has an orthogonal basis $e_1, \dots, e_n$ with $e_i^{\,2} \mathrel{:=} Q(e_i) = +1$ for $p$ vectors and $-1$ for the remaining $q = n-p$; the \emph{signature} $(p,q)$ is an invariant (Sylvester), and is \emph{mixed} when $p, q \geq 1$.

The \emph{Clifford algebra} $\Cl(p,q) = \Cl(\mathbb{V}, Q)$ is generated by $\mathbb{V}$ subject to $v^2 = Q(v)$. Polarising gives $ab + ba = 2\,a \cdot b$, so orthogonal vectors anticommute; $ab = a \cdot b + a \wedge b$ with $a \wedge b \mathrel{:=} \tfrac12(ab-ba)$ the \emph{outer product}, pure grade two. The ordered products $e_{i_1} \cdots e_{i_k}$ over an orthogonal basis, $i_1 < \dots < i_k$, the \emph{basis blades} with $1$ as the empty product, form a linear basis, so $\dim \Cl(\mathbb{V},Q) = 2^n$; this holds for degenerate forms too \cite{Chevalley1997}, which we need once (Lemma \claimref{transport.splitting-along-hyperbolic-plane}). An element has \emph{grade} $k$ if it combines blades of length $k$, basis-independently \cite{Porteous1995}. A vector with $Q(v) \neq 0$ is invertible, $v^{-1} = v/Q(v)$; a nonzero vector with $Q(v) = 0$ is \emph{null}, and null vectors exist exactly in mixed signature, where they form a cone \cite[Sections 2 to 4]{ButlerT0}. A word on the two notations: we write $\Cl(p,q)$ whenever only the signature matters, and $\Cl(\mathbb{V})$ or $\Cl(\mathbb{V}')$ for the algebra of a \emph{specific} quadratic space, chiefly an extension quantified over in a theorem, whose form is not assumed nondegenerate and so may carry no signature label at all.
__notes__.note.transport.setting-symmetry-action-e: Equivariance is the precise form of ``respecting the symmetries'': if two null vectors are related by a symmetry of the space, their assigned partners must be related by the same symmetry. The consequence used below is the case of a stabiliser: if $g$ fixes $v$ then $\sigma(v) = \tau_g(\sigma(v))$.
__notes__.note.transport.setting-type-p-rule-no-ru: Do non-central idempotents demand an ascent? The answer is that type P demands nothing, and the reason is a one-line identity whose \emph{absence} is precisely what made type N hard. We state the repair theorem in the exact form of the no-go of the section “The refuted conjecture, and the no-go”, so that the two answers can be compared clause by clause; then we develop the structure theory that shows the triviality is a theorem about the idempotent variety, not an evasion of it.
__notes__.note.transport.setting-repair-theorem-co: An idempotent $e \notin \{0,1\}$ is a genuine invertibility obstruction: $e(1-e) = 0$ exhibits it as a zero divisor, and it has no inverse in any unital extension (if $ex = 1$ then $e = e(ex) = e^2 x = ex = 1$). The transport question of the section “The refuted conjecture, and the no-go”, transposed verbatim from the null cone to the idempotent variety, is therefore well posed: does some extension of the algebra carry an equivariant assignment of von Neumann pseudo-inverses to the idempotents? For null vectors the answer was no, in every extension. For idempotents:
__notes__.note.transport.setting-idempotent-variet: The repair theorem shows type P poses no transport problem; the following classification shows why it could not have: a type-P idempotent carries no invariant data beyond its rank, so any two candidates of the same rank are the same candidate up to gauge.

obj.transport.equivariance.formal:
Let $\mathbb{V}' \supseteq \mathbb{V}$ be an extension of quadratic spaces (Definition \claimref{obj.transport.extension-quadratic-spaces}) and $G$ a subgroup of $\Pin(p,q)$, acting on the null cone $\Ncone \subset \mathbb{V}$ by $\Ad$ (which preserves $\mathbb{V}$ and its null cone, being an isometry of $\mathbb{V}$) and on $\Cl(\mathbb{V}')$ by $\tau$ through the inclusion $\Cl(\mathbb{V}) \subseteq \Cl(\mathbb{V}')$. A map $\sigma : \Ncone \to \Cl(\mathbb{V}')$ is \emph{$G$-equivariant} if
\[
\sigma\bigl(\Ad_g(v)\bigr) \;=\; \tau_g\bigl(\sigma(v)\bigr) \qquad \text{for all } g \in G,\ v \in \Ncone .
\]
obj.transport.equivariance.technical:
Given an extension $\mathbb{V}' \supseteq \mathbb{V}$ of quadratic spaces and a subgroup $G$ of $\Pin(p,q)$, the group acts on the null cone $\Ncone \subset \mathbb{V}$ by $\Ad$, which is an isometry of $\mathbb{V}$ and so preserves $\Ncone$, and acts on $\Cl(\mathbb{V}')$ by $\tau$ through the inclusion $\Cl(\mathbb{V}) \subseteq \Cl(\mathbb{V}')$. A map $\sigma : \Ncone \to \Cl(\mathbb{V}')$ is $G$-equivariant when $\sigma(\Ad_g(v)) = \tau_g(\sigma(v))$ for all $g \in G$ and all null $v$.

This is the sense in which a rule assigning an algebra element to each null vector is required to respect the symmetry of the geometry: transforming the input by $g$ transforms the output by the same $g$.
obj.transport.equivariance.lay: A rule that attaches something to each light-like direction is called equivariant if it does not depend on how the geometry is oriented. Moving the geometry by a symmetry and then applying the rule gives the same answer as applying the rule first and then moving the answer. The symmetries are those of the original space, acting also on the algebra of any enlargement of it.

obj.transport.obstruction-types.technical:
In a nondegenerate $A = \Cl(p,q)$ a zero-divisor obstruction is of one of three types. Type N is a nonzero null vector $v$, $Q(v) = 0$, together with the annihilating idempotent $wv$ it acquires through a hyperbolic partner $w$: geometrically an isotropic line, a direction without a metric partner. Type P is a non-central idempotent $e = e^2$ with $e 
otin \{0, 1\}$, prototype $e = 	frac12(1 + u)$ with $u^2 = 1$, $u 
eq \pm 1$; it is a zero divisor through $e(1 - e) = 0$.

Type C is a central idempotent $e 
otin \{0, 1\}$. Then the two-sided ideals $eA$ and $(1 - e)A$ annihilate one another and $A = eA \oplus (1 - e)A$.
obj.transport.obstruction-types.lay: Division can fail in a Clifford algebra in three different ways, and this definition names them. Type N is a direction of zero length, such as a light ray in spacetime. Type P is an element that equals its own square without being 0 or 1, like a projection that keeps part of a space and discards the rest. Type C is such a projection that commutes with everything, which means the whole algebra falls apart into two independent pieces.

rule2.which-residues-obstruct-which-way.formal: The even residues whose spacelike extension is type C are $\{2, 6\}$; those whose timelike extension is type C are $\{0, 4\}$. In particular every even residue has exactly one obstructing one-dimensional extension. The physical lineage sits at residue $6$ and its Rule 1 ascents never leave it (Fact \claimref{transport.rule-1-morita-trivial}); by Theorem \claimref{rule2.where-obstruction-sits-commuting-square} it leaves residue $6$ only through a spacelike Kaluza-Klein direction, into the obstruction at residue $5$, and the opposite-sign repair returns it to $6$ as $\Mat_2$ of where it started. The same holds at the mirror residue $2$, with spacelike read as square $-1$ in both towers: in T14's causal convention, where the mirror's time is its minus sign, that extension is the mirror's second time, and the mirror's own Kaluza-Klein direction gives the unobstructed $\Cl(4,1)$ (Proposition \claimref{synthesis.mirror-extensions-causal-convention}).
rule2.which-residues-obstruct-which-way.technical:
For an even-dimensional $\Cl(p,q)$ with residue $d = p - q \bmod 8$, the spacelike one-dimensional extension carries the type-C obstruction exactly when $d \in \{2, 6\}$ and the timelike one exactly when $d \in \{0, 4\}$, so every even residue has exactly one obstructing one-dimensional extension. Using that Rule 1 ascents preserve the residue, the physical lineage at $d = 6$ leaves residue $6$ only through a spacelike Kaluza-Klein direction, into the type-C obstruction at residue $5$.

The Rule 2 repair of that obstruction by a generator of the opposite sign returns it to residue $6$ as $\Mat_2$ of the algebra it started from. The mirror residue $2$ behaves in the same way when spacelike means square $-1$; in T14's causal convention that obstructing extension is the mirror's second time, not its Kaluza-Klein direction.
rule2.which-residues-obstruct-which-way.lay: Clifford algebras repeat in a cycle of eight, so each one has a residue from 0 to 7. The physical case sits at residue 6: its only exit is an extra space direction, and repairing that break with a direction of the opposite kind brings it back to residue 6 as two-by-two matrices over where it began.

singularity.imported-no-c-number-repair.formal: No equivariant assignment of classical partner values to the dying directions exists, in the minimal ascent or in any enlargement. Mechanism: the stabiliser of the null direction $[v]$ contains the parabolic null rotations, the candidate partners form an affine space on which those rotations act by translation, and a translation of an affine space has no fixed point; cohomologically, the obstruction is the tautological class of the unipotent stabiliser, nonzero in every mixed-signature dimension above two. \emph{Provenance:} the element-level no-go is \cite[Thm.~4.2]{ButlerT1}; the totality of the transported division is \cite[Thm.~4.10]{ButlerT1}; the cohomological form, with the torsor made exact modulo the left ideal and the class identified as $\theta \in H^1(N_v; U) = \operatorname{Hom}(N_v, U)$, is \cite[Thm.~4.8]{ButlerT1}. The dimension-two exception, where the class vanishes, is exactly Lemma \claimref{singularity.pseudo-inverse-identities-hyperbolic-atom}'s self-completeness. \emph{Scope:} these theorems are proved where the ambient form is nondegenerate and the dying direction has a hyperbolic partner, which is the situation at every point of the invertible region, whose limits toward $E$ the no-go therefore governs; at $E$ itself the partner is exactly what is missing (Proposition \claimref{singularity.type-n-only-type-n}), so the import does not apply there verbatim. singularity.pseudo-inverse-identities-hy.formal:
From $v^2 = (v^*)^2 = 0, \qquad v v^* + v^* v = 1$ alone: $v v^* v = v$ and $v^* v v^* = v^*$, so each member of the pair is a von Neumann pseudo-inverse of the other, with no genuine inverse existing ($v$ is a zero divisor). The pair is realisable inside a single $(1,1)$ block: in $\Cl(1,1)$ with $e_0^2 = 1$, $e_1^2 = -1$, the vectors
\[
v = \tfrac12(e_0 + e_1), \qquad v^* = \tfrac12(e_0 - e_1)
\]
satisfy $v^2 = (v^*)^2 = 0, \qquad v v^* + v^* v = 1$ exactly. This block, the \emph{hyperbolic atom}, is the unique unit of transport that, at the level of elements, needs no ascent of its own \cite[Rem.~4.5]{ButlerT1}.
singularity.pseudo-inverse-identities-hy.technical:
Let $v, v^*$ satisfy the canonical anticommutation relations $v^2 = (v^*)^2 = 0$ and $v v^* + v^* v = 1$. These relations alone give $v v^* v = v$ and $v^* v v^* = v^*$, so each member of the pair is a von Neumann pseudo-inverse of the other, although no genuine inverse exists because $v$ is a zero divisor.

The pair is realised exactly inside a single $(1,1)$ block: in $\Cl(1,1)$ with $Q(e_0) = 1$ and $Q(e_1) = -1$, take $v = \tfrac12(e_0 + e_1)$ and $v^* = \tfrac12(e_0 - e_1)$. This block, the hyperbolic atom, is the unique unit of transport that, at the level of elements, needs no ascent of its own.
singularity.pseudo-inverse-identities-hy.lay: Two elements that each square to zero can still act as partial inverses of one another: multiplying one by the other and then by the first again returns the first. Neither has a true inverse. Such a pair already lives in the algebra of a single plane with one space-like and one time-like direction, called the hyperbolic atom, which is the one building block of transport that, at the level of elements, needs no ascent of its own.

transport.cohomological-form-no-go.technical:
Let $v$ be a null vector with hyperbolic partner, $U$ the orthogonal complement of the hyperbolic plane in $\mathbb{V}$, and $N_v \cong (U, +)$ the group of null rotations fixing $v$. With trivial coefficients $H^1(N_v; U) = \mathrm{Hom}(N_v, U)$, and the class of the pseudo-inverse torsor is the tautological homomorphism $\theta$, nonzero whenever $U \neq 0$. An $N_v$-invariant pseudo-inverse of $v$ exists in a given extension if and only if this class vanishes, if and only if $U = 0$, that is $n = 2$, the hyperbolic atom.

Three consequences follow. $N_v$, $U$ and $\theta$ are built inside $\Cl(\mathbb{V})$, so the obstruction is pulled back unchanged along every ascent; $\theta$ intertwines the conjugation action of $\Spin(U)$ on $N_v$ with its vector action on $U$; and any subgroup of the stabiliser of $v$ containing $N_v$, including the full parabolic stabiliser of $[v]$, is obstructed at once.
transport.cohomological-form-no-go.lay: Earlier results show that the symmetries fixing a light-like direction slide every candidate partial inverse along by a definite amount. This theorem packages that sliding as a single algebraic invariant, which vanishes only in the smallest case of one space and one time direction. Because the invariant is built inside the original algebra, enlarging the algebra or the symmetry group cannot remove it.

transport.exceptional-division-algebras.technical:
$\Cl(p,q)$ has no zero divisors exactly when $(p,q) \in \{(0,0), (0,1), (0,2)\}$, where it is $\R$, $\C$ or $\HH$. It has no nilpotents exactly for those three together with $\Cl(1,0) \cong \R \oplus \R$ and $\Cl(0,3) \cong \HH \oplus \HH$.

Both lists are read off the classification of real Clifford algebras: a matrix algebra $\Mat_k(\mathbb{F})$ with $k \geq 2$ contains the nilpotent matrix unit $E_{12}$, a direct sum contains the zero divisors $(x, 0)$, a division algebra contains neither, and a dimension count fixes the signatures.
transport.exceptional-division-algebras.lay: In most Clifford algebras some nonzero elements multiply to zero, so division sometimes fails. This result lists the only exceptions: the real numbers, the complex numbers and the quaternions. transport.exhaustiveness-every-zero-divi.formal:
Let $A = \Cl(p,q)$ be nondegenerate, $a \in A$ a nonzero zero divisor. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item There exist idempotents $e, f \notin \{0, 1\}$ with $a(1-e) = 0$ and $(1-f)a = 0$ (so $a$ both left-annihilates and is right-annihilated by nontrivial idempotents).
\item If $p - q \not\equiv 1 \pmod 4$, every such idempotent is non-central: the obstruction carried by $a$ is of type P, refined to type N exactly when the annihilating idempotent is the $wv$ of a hyperbolic pair, as in Example \claimref{note.transport.hyperbolic-partner-supplies-annihilating-idempotent}.
\item If $p - q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, the element $a$ may in addition be annihilated by a \emph{central} idempotent (this happens exactly when $\varepsilon_+ a = 0$ or $\varepsilon_- a = 0$, i.e.\ when $a$ lies entirely in one simple ideal): type C. Every zero divisor not of this kind is again of type P within its ideal(s).
\end{enumerate}
Consequently the taxonomy N/P/C of Definition \claimref{obj.transport.obstruction-types} is exhaustive: every failure of invertibility in a real Clifford algebra of nondegenerate form is localised at an idempotent, non-central in the simple signatures, possibly central exactly in the signatures $p - q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, and of isotropic-vector origin exactly in the mixed signatures.
transport.exhaustiveness-every-zero-divi.technical:
Let $A = \Cl(p,q)$ be nondegenerate and $a 
eq 0$ a zero divisor. Then there are idempotents $e, f 
otin \{0, 1\}$ with $a(1 - e) = 0$ and $(1 - f)a = 0$. If $p - q 
ot\equiv 1 \pmod 4$ every such idempotent is non-central, so the obstruction is type P, refined to type N exactly when the annihilating idempotent is $wv$ for a hyperbolic pair. If $p - q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, $a$ may also be annihilated by a central idempotent, which happens exactly when $a$ lies entirely in one simple ideal (type C); otherwise it is again type P within its ideals.

So the taxonomy N, P, C is exhaustive: every failure of invertibility is localised at an idempotent, non-central in the simple signatures, possibly central exactly when $p - q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, and of isotropic-vector origin exactly in the mixed signatures.
transport.exhaustiveness-every-zero-divi.lay: Whenever division fails in a Clifford algebra with a nondegenerate notion of length, the failure can be traced to an element that equals its own square. This shows that the three kinds of failure already named cover every case. Which kinds occur depends only on the numbers of space and time directions.

transport.existence-classification-type-.formal:
$\Cl(p,q)$ ($n \geq 1$) contains a nontrivial central idempotent if and only if
\[
p - q \equiv 1 \pmod 4 ,
\]
and in that case the nontrivial central idempotents are exactly the two elements
\[
\varepsilon_\pm = \tfrac12\,(1 \pm \omega),
\]
which are exchanged by the grade involution $\hat{\cdot}$ (an \emph{outer} automorphism of the split algebra; no inner automorphism exchanges them, centrality being conjugation-invariant), and satisfy $\varepsilon_+ \varepsilon_- = 0$ and $\varepsilon_+ + \varepsilon_- = 1$, and effect the splitting $\Cl(p,q) = \varepsilon_+ A \,\oplus\, \varepsilon_- A$ into the two simple ideals of Theorem \claimref{transport.classification-real-clifford-algebras}.
transport.existence-classification-type-.technical:
A type C obstruction is a nontrivial central idempotent, so it must lie in the centre, which is $\R$ for even $n$ and $\R[\omega]$ for odd $n$. When $\omega^2 = -1$ that centre is a copy of $\C$, whose only idempotents are $0$ and $1$; when $\omega^2 = +1$ it is $\R \oplus \R$, with exactly two nontrivial idempotents $\varepsilon_\pm = \tfrac12(1 \pm \omega)$. Combining the parity of $n$ with the sign of $\omega^2$ shows that $\Cl(p,q)$, $n \geq 1$, has a nontrivial central idempotent if and only if $p - q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$.

In that case $\varepsilon_+ \varepsilon_- = 0$ and $\varepsilon_+ + \varepsilon_- = 1$, and $\Cl(p,q) = \varepsilon_+ A \oplus \varepsilon_- A$ is the splitting into two simple ideals. The grade involution sends $\omega \mapsto -\omega$ and so exchanges $\varepsilon_+$ and $\varepsilon_-$; it is an outer automorphism, because an inner automorphism fixes every central element and therefore cannot exchange them.
transport.existence-classification-type-.lay: Some Clifford algebras secretly come in two independent halves, and the elements that pick out each half are called central idempotents. This result pins down exactly when that happens: precisely when the number of positive directions minus the number of negative ones leaves remainder 1 on division by four. In that case there are exactly two such elements, built from the product of all the basis directions. Reversing every direction swaps the two halves, but no conjugation by an element of the algebra itself can do so, since these elements commute with everything.
transport.existence-classification-type-.typing_note: kept all three edges; the centre and sign lemmas drive the existence proof and the classification supplies the simplicity of the two ideals asserted in the statement

proofs.main: A central idempotent lies in the centre $\Zc$, computed in Lemma \claimref{transport.centre}. If $n$ is even, $\Zc = \R$, whose idempotents are $0$ and $1$: no type C. If $n$ is odd, $\Zc = \R[\omega]$ with $\omega^2 = \pm 1$ by Lemma \claimref{transport.sign}. Case $\omega^2 = -1$: $\Zc \cong \C$, and an idempotent $a + b\omega$ satisfies $a^2 - b^2 = a$ and $2ab = b$; if $b \neq 0$ the second gives $a = \tfrac12$ and the first $-b^2 = \tfrac14$, impossible over $\R$; so $b = 0$ and $a \in \{0,1\}$: no type C. Case $\omega^2 = +1$: $\Zc \cong \R \oplus \R$ via $\varepsilon_\pm$, whose idempotents are $0, 1, \varepsilon_+, \varepsilon_-$; direct check $\varepsilon_\pm^2 = \tfrac14(1 \pm 2\omega + \omega^2) = \varepsilon_\pm$ and $\varepsilon_+\varepsilon_- = \tfrac14(1 - \omega^2) = 0$. By Lemma \claimref{transport.sign}, $n$ odd and $\omega^2 = +1$ happen together precisely when $p - q$ is odd and $p - q \equiv 0, 1 \pmod 4$, i.e.\ precisely when $p - q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$. For the exchange: for $n$ odd the pseudoscalar is central, so no inner automorphism, in particular no vector conjugation, moves it; the exchanging symmetry must instead be the \emph{grade involution}: $\hat{\omega} = (-1)^n \omega = -\omega$ for $n$ odd (\claimref{std-algebra.involution-properties}), so the grade involution, implemented on the algebra by conjugation in the larger algebra $\Cl(p,q{+}1)$ or realised abstractly as an outer automorphism, exchanges $\varepsilon_+ \leftrightarrow \varepsilon_-$. Within $A$ itself the two ideals are exchanged by no inner automorphism, centrality being conjugation-invariant, and this is exactly why type C is the deepest obstruction: no inner automorphism can act on it. The splitting into two simple ideals is Theorem \claimref{transport.classification-real-clifford-algebras} ($d \in \{1,5\}$), each ideal $\varepsilon_\pm A \cong \Mat_k(\mathbb{F})$.

transport.existence-locus-type-n.formal: $\Cl(p,q)$ contains a null vector if and only if the signature is mixed, $pq \neq 0$. In that case the null vectors form a cone of dimension $n - 1$, and every null vector is a two-sided zero divisor without left or right inverse in any unital algebra containing $\Cl(p,q)$.
transport.existence-locus-type-n.technical:
A null vector is a nonzero $v$ with $Q(v) = 0$. In $\Cl(p,q)$ such vectors exist exactly when the signature is mixed, $pq \neq 0$: a definite form is anisotropic, while for $p, q \geq 1$ the sum of a positive and a negative unit basis vector is null. When they exist, the null vectors form a cone of dimension $n - 1$, the zero set of the quadratic form with the origin removed.

Every null vector satisfies $v^2 = 0$ and so is a two-sided zero divisor, and it has neither a left nor a right inverse in any unital algebra containing $\Cl(p,q)$: from $vw = 1$ one would get $v = v^2 w = 0$.
transport.existence-locus-type-n.lay: In a space with both positive and negative directions, like the space-time of relativity, there are nonzero directions of zero length, called null directions. This result says they exist exactly when both kinds of direction are present, and that they then form a cone, much like a light cone. Each such direction multiplied by itself gives zero, so it can never be divided by, even in a larger algebra that contains the original one.
transport.existence-locus-type-n.typing_note: kept the no-inverse lemma, which the proof cites for non-invertibility in every extension

proofs.main: If $q = 0$ or $p = 0$ the form is definite and anisotropic: $Q(v) = 0$ forces $v = 0$. Non-invertibility in every extension is Lemma \claimref{transport.noinverse}: from $v^2 = 0$, $vw = 1$ gives $v = v^2 w = 0$.
