transport.existence-locus-type-p.formal:
$\Cl(p,q)$ contains a non-central idempotent if and only if it is not a direct sum of division algebras, that is, if and only if
\[
(p,q) \;\notin\; \{(0,0),\ (0,1),\ (0,2),\ (1,0),\ (0,3)\} .
\]
In particular, for $n \geq 2$ with $(p,q) \notin \{(0,2), (0,3)\}$, type P is always present, and concretely: any invertible vector pair $a, b$ with $a \cdot b = 0$ and $a^2 b^2 = -1$ (one timelike and one spacelike factor) yields the non-central idempotent $\tfrac12(1 + u)$ with $u = ab$, since then $(ab)^2 = -a^2b^2 = +1$, and every unit blade $u$ with $u^2 = 1$, $u \neq \pm 1$, $u$ non-central yields one.
transport.existence-locus-type-p.technical:
$\Cl(p,q)$ contains a non-central idempotent exactly when it is not a direct sum of division algebras, that is when $(p,q) 
otin \{(0,0), (0,1), (0,2), (1,0), (0,3)\}$. In particular, for $n \geq 2$ with $(p,q) 
otin \{(0,2), (0,3)\}$ type P is always present.

Concretely, orthogonal invertible vectors $a, b$ with $Q(a)Q(b) = -1$, one timelike and one spacelike, give $u = ab$ with $u^2 = -Q(a)Q(b) = 1$ and hence the non-central idempotent $	frac12(1 + u)$; more generally every non-central unit blade $u$ with $u^2 = 1$, $u 
eq \pm 1$, yields one.
transport.existence-locus-type-p.lay: An element that equals its own square but does not commute with everything is a type-P obstruction. Such elements exist in every real Clifford algebra except five small ones built from the real numbers, the complex numbers and the quaternions. A simple recipe produces one from a space-like and a time-like direction at right angles.
transport.existence-locus-type-p.typing_note: Added the classification of real Clifford algebras, which the proof invokes directly for the matrix-algebra case and for existence in every listed signature.

proofs.main: In a division algebra, and in a sum of two, every idempotent is a sum of the componentwise trivial ones, hence central: $(x,y)$ idempotent in $D_1 \oplus D_2$ forces $x \in \{0,1\}$, $y \in \{0,1\}$, all four combinations central. Conversely if $\Cl(p,q) \cong \Mat_k(\mathbb{F})$ (or a sum) with $k \geq 2$, the matrix unit $E_{11}$ is a non-central idempotent. The signature list is Proposition \claimref{transport.exceptional-division-algebras}. For the concrete form: if $u^2 = 1$ then $\tfrac12(1+u)$ is idempotent, and it is central iff $u$ is; a product of two orthogonal invertible vectors squares to $(ab)^2 = -a^2b^2 = +1$ (\claimref{std-algebra.orthogonal-anticommute}) iff $a^2 b^2 = -1$, i.e.\ one timelike and one spacelike factor, available whenever $pq \neq 0$; in definite signature take instead a grade-one unit $u = e_1$ with $e_1^2 = +1$ ($p \geq 1$), or in the negative-definite case a suitable blade, e.g.\ $u = e_1e_2e_3e_4$ with $u^2 = +1$ for $q \geq 4$; the classification (\claimref{transport.classification-real-clifford-algebras}) guarantees existence in all listed cases, the explicit blade being a convenience, not the proof.

transport.group-null-rotations.formal:
Let $v$ be a null vector with hyperbolic partner $w$ and $U = \{v, w\}^{\perp}$ the nondegenerate complement of the plane they span. For $u \in U$ set $R_u = 1 + vu$. Then $R_u R_{u'} = R_{u + u'}$, so
\[
N_v \;=\; \{\, R_u : u \in U \,\}
\]
is an abelian subgroup of $\Spin^0(p,q)$, and $u \mapsto R_u$ is an isomorphism of groups $(U, +) \cong N_v$. Each $R_u$ fixes $v$. Moreover the assignment is equivariant for the Levi factor: every rotor $g$ in the even subalgebra of $\Cl(U)$ fixes $v$ and satisfies $g\, R_u\, g^{-1} = R_{g u g^{-1}}$, the conjugation on the right being the vector action of $\Spin(U)$ on $U$.
transport.group-null-rotations.technical:
Let $v$ be a null vector with hyperbolic partner and $U$ the nondegenerate complement of the hyperbolic plane. For $u \in U$ put $R_u = 1 + vu$. Then $R_u R_{u'} = R_{u + u'}$, so $N_v = \{R_u : u \in U\}$ is an abelian subgroup of $\Spin^0(p,q)$ and $u \mapsto R_u$ is a group isomorphism $(U, +) \cong N_v$; each $R_u$ fixes $v$.

The isomorphism is equivariant for the Levi factor: every rotor $g$ in the even subalgebra of $\Cl(U)$ fixes $v$ and satisfies $g R_u g^{-1} = R_{g u g^{-1}}$, where $u \mapsto g u g^{-1}$ is the vector action of $\Spin(U)$ on $U$.
transport.group-null-rotations.lay: Among the symmetries of a space with both space and time directions, some leave a chosen light-like direction exactly in place while shearing other directions along it. These null rotations combine just as vectors add in the directions perpendicular to the light ray and its partner. Ordinary rotations of those perpendicular directions act on the null rotations in the expected way.

proofs.main: $R_u R_{u'} = 1 + v(u + u') + vuvu'$, and $vuvu' = (vuv)u' = 0$ since $vuv = -v^2u = 0$; so the group law holds, with $R_0 = 1$ and $R_u^{-1} = R_{-u}$. Injectivity of $u \mapsto R_u$: $vu = v \wedge u \neq 0$ for $u \neq 0$ by the blade basis (\claimref{std-algebra.blade-basis}). Membership in $\Spin^0$ and the fixing of $v$ are Step 2 of the proof of Theorem \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements}. For the Levi statement: $g$ is an even product of vectors of $U$, each anticommuting with $v$ (\claimref{std-algebra.orthogonal-anticommute}), so $g$ commutes with $v$ and $gvg^{-1} = v$; then $g R_u g^{-1} = 1 + (gvg^{-1})(gug^{-1}) = 1 + v\,(gug^{-1})$, and $gug^{-1} \in U$ is the rotor action.

transport.no-go-level-elements.formal: Let $(\mathbb{V}, Q)$ be nondegenerate of mixed signature $(p,q)$, $p, q \geq 1$, with $n = p + q \geq 3$, and let $\Ncone \subset \mathbb{V}$ be its null cone. Let $(\mathbb{V}', Q')$ be \emph{any} extension of $(\mathbb{V}, Q)$ in the sense of Definition \claimref{obj.transport.extension-quadratic-spaces}, possibly $\mathbb{V}$ itself. Then there is no map $\sigma : \Ncone \to \Cl(\mathbb{V}')$ satisfying $v\,\sigma(v)\,v = v$ for every null $v$ that is equivariant, in the sense of Definition \claimref{obj.transport.equivariance}, even under the identity component $\Spin^0(p,q)$; a fortiori none equivariant under $\Spin(p,q)$ or $\Pin(p,q)$. Equivariant division by zero is impossible at the level of elements, in the Clifford algebra of every ascent, however large.
transport.no-go-level-elements.technical:
Let $(\mathbb{V}, Q)$ be nondegenerate of mixed signature $(p,q)$, $p, q \geq 1$, with $n = p + q \geq 3$ and null cone $\Ncone$, and let $\mathbb{V}'$ be any extension of $\mathbb{V}$, possibly $\mathbb{V}$ itself. Then no map $\sigma : \Ncone \to \Cl(\mathbb{V}')$ with $v\,\sigma(v)\,v = v$ for every null $v$ is equivariant even under $\Spin^0(p,q)$, and a fortiori none is equivariant under $\Spin(p,q)$ or $\Pin(p,q)$.

The proof puts every pseudo-inverse in the normal form $w_0 + \alpha + v\beta + v w_0\delta$ relative to a hyperbolic pair $(v, w_0)$ and conjugates by a null rotation $R = 1 + vu$. This fixes $v$ but shifts the $\Cl(U')$-component by $-u$, so equivariance would force $u = 0$ for every $u \in U$ with $Q(u) \neq 0$, which is impossible.
transport.no-go-level-elements.lay: A light-like direction has no inverse, but it has many partial inverses. This theorem shows that there is no way to choose one for every light-like direction that respects the symmetries of the geometry, in any space with both space and time directions and at least three dimensions. Enlarging the algebra by any number of new directions does not help.

proofs.main:
Fix a null $v \in \Ncone$ and a null partner $w_0$ with $v \cdot w_0 = \tfrac12$, by the hyperbolic-pair construction of the section “Null vectors, zero divisors, and hyperbolic planes” (\claimref{std-algebra.witt-decomposition}); write $H_0 = \mathrm{span}\{v, w_0\}$ and $U = \{v, w_0\}^{\perp} \cap \mathbb{V}$, a nondegenerate subspace of $\mathbb{V}$ of dimension $n - 2 \geq 1$. By Definition \claimref{obj.transport.extension-quadratic-spaces} the extension splits as $\mathbb{V}' = \mathbb{V} \perp \mathbb{V}^{\perp}$, so
\[
\mathbb{V}' \;=\; H_0 \perp U', \qquad U' \mathrel{:=} U \perp \mathbb{V}^{\perp},
\]
and Lemma \claimref{transport.splitting-along-hyperbolic-plane} applies: every candidate $\sigma = \sigma(v) \in \Cl(\mathbb{V}')$ has a unique expansion $\sigma = \alpha + v\beta + w_0\gamma + v w_0 \delta$ with $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta \in \Cl(U')$. Throughout, $\hat{\cdot}$ is the grade involution and we use the commutation rule $v\,x = \hat{x}\,v, \qquad x\,v = v\,\hat{x}$ (Lemma \claimref{primer.commutation-rule}) for $v$ against $\Cl(U')$, together with the hyperbolic-pair identities $v^2 = w^2 = 0, \qquad vw + wv = 1, \qquad \text{hence} \quad vwv = (1 - wv)v = v$.

\emph{Step 1 (normal form for pseudo-inverses).} Compute $v\sigma v$ term by term:
\[
v\,\alpha\, v = v\, (\alpha v) = v\,(v \hat{\alpha}) = v^2 \hat\alpha = 0, \qquad
v\,(v\beta)\,v = v^2 \beta v = 0, \qquad
v\,(v w_0 \delta)\,v = v^2 w_0 \delta v = 0,
\]
while the third term survives:
\[
v\,(w_0 \gamma)\,v \;=\; v w_0\,(\gamma v) \;=\; v w_0\, v \hat{\gamma} \;=\; v \hat{\gamma}
\]
by $v^2 = w^2 = 0, \qquad vw + wv = 1, \qquad \text{hence} \quad vwv = (1 - wv)v = v$. Hence $v \sigma v = v \hat{\gamma}$, and since left multiplication by $v$ is injective on $\Cl(U')$ (Lemma \claimref{transport.splitting-along-hyperbolic-plane}(2)) and $\hat{\cdot}$ is an involution, $v \sigma v = v$ holds if and only if $\gamma = 1$. Every pseudo-inverse of $v$ therefore has the form
\[
\sigma \;=\; w_0 + \alpha + v\beta + v w_0 \delta .
\]
Note that only the first von Neumann identity is used; the theorem does not even require $\sigma v \sigma = \sigma$.

\emph{Step 2 (null rotations).} For $u \in U$ set $R = 1 + vu$. Since $v \cdot u = 0$ and $v^2 = 0$,
\[
(vu)^2 = v\,(uv)\,u = -v\,(vu)\,u = -v^2 u^2 = 0, \qquad \text{and in particular} \quad vuv = -v^2u = 0,
\]
so $R = \exp(vu) = \exp(v \wedge u)$, with $R^{-1} = 1 - vu$. $R$ is even, and its reverse is $\widetilde{R} = 1 + uv = 1 - vu = R^{-1}$, so $R \widetilde{R} = 1$ and $R$ is a rotor.

Take from now on $u$ with $Q(u) \neq 0$, which is possible because $U$ is nondegenerate and nonzero; such $u$ span $U$. Then $R$ is a versor outright, not merely a rotor. Indeed the vector $u' \mathrel{:=} u + Q(u)\,v$ satisfies $Q(u') = Q(u) + 2Q(u)\,(u \cdot v) = Q(u) \neq 0$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:versorfactor}
u'u \;=\; u^2 + Q(u)\,vu \;=\; Q(u)\,(1 + vu), \qquad \text{so} \qquad R \;=\; \frac{u'\,u}{Q(u)},
\end{equation}
a product of two invertible vectors of equal square. Normalising both factors to unit square multiplies the product by $|Q(u)|/Q(u) = \pm 1$, and when that sign is $-1$ we have $Q(u) < 0$, so the normalised $\hat{u} = u/\sqrt{|Q(u)|}$ satisfies $\hat{u}^2 = -1$ and the sign is itself a product of unit vectors. Hence $R \in \Spin(p,q)$. The same factorisation applies with $u$ replaced by $tu$ for every $t \neq 0$, so $t \mapsto 1 + t\,vu$ is a continuous path \emph{inside the group} joining $1$ to $R$, and therefore $R \in \Spin^0(p,q)$.

Its action on vectors is computed directly. On $v$:
\[
R\,v\,R^{-1} = (1 + vu)\,v\,(1 - vu) = (v + vuv)(1 - vu) = v(1 - vu) = v - v^2u = v ,
\]
so $R$ fixes $v$. On $u'' \in U'$, using $u''v = -vu''$, $u u'' v = v u u''$ (two anticommutations) and $vuv = 0$:
\[
R\,u''\,R^{-1} = u'' - u''vu + vuu'' - vuu''vu = u'' + v(u''u + uu'') - v(vuu'')u = u'' + 2(u \cdot u'')\,v .
\]
On $w_0$, using $w_0 v = 1 - v w_0$ and $u w_0 = -w_0 u$:
\[
vuw_0 - w_0vu = -vw_0u - (1 - vw_0)u = -u, \qquad
vuw_0vu = vu(1 - vw_0)u = vu^2 - (vuv)w_0u = Q(u)\,v,
\]
whence
\[
R\,w_0\,R^{-1} = w_0 + (vuw_0 - w_0vu) - vuw_0vu = w_0 - u - Q(u)\,v .
\]
These are the \emph{null rotations}, the parabolic transvections stabilising the null direction $v$.

\emph{Step 3 (the shear).} Conjugate the normal form of Step 1 by $R$ and collect the $\Cl(U')$-component, i.e.\ the coefficient of $1 \in \Cl(H_0)$ in the unique expansion of Lemma \claimref{transport.splitting-along-hyperbolic-plane}. Term by term, using $\alpha v = v\hat\alpha$, $\delta v = v \hat\delta$, $\beta v = v\hat\beta$ and $vuv = 0$:
\begin{align*}
R\,\alpha\,R^{-1} &= \alpha + vu\alpha - \alpha vu - vu\alpha vu
= \alpha + v\,(u\alpha - \hat{\alpha}u) && (\alpha vu = v\hat\alpha u;\ vu\alpha v = vuv\hat\alpha = 0),\\
R\,(v\beta)\,R^{-1} &= v\beta + (vuv)\beta - (v\beta v)u - (vuv)\beta vu = v\beta && (v\beta v = v^2\hat\beta = 0),\\
R\,(v w_0 \delta)\,R^{-1} &= v w_0 \delta - v w_0 \delta v u = v w_0 \delta - v\hat{\delta}u && (v w_0 \delta v u = v w_0 v \hat{\delta} u = v \hat\delta u),\\
R\,w_0\,R^{-1} &= w_0 - u - Q(u)\,v && \text{(Step 2)}.
\end{align*}
Every correction except one retains a left factor of $v$ and therefore lies in the $v$- or $vw_0$-slots of the expansion; the sole contribution to the $\Cl(U')$-component comes from $R w_0 R^{-1}$, and that component of $R\,\sigma(v)\,R^{-1}$ equals $\alpha - u$. But $R$ fixes $v$, so equivariance demands $\tau_R(\sigma(v)) = R\,\sigma(v)\,R^{-1} = \sigma(v)$; comparing $\Cl(U')$-components in the unique expansion gives $\alpha - u = \alpha$, i.e.\ $u = 0$, for \emph{every} $u \in U$ with $Q(u) \neq 0$. Since $U$ is nondegenerate of dimension $n - 2 \geq 1$, such $u$ exist, a contradiction.

transport.no-transport-terminates.formal: No algebra reachable by a nonempty transport history is free of zero divisors. Every Rule-1 completion has mixed signature and so carries type N; indeed the adjoined pair $f, f^*$ is itself null: the repair of the old null cone is effected by adjoining new members of it. Every Rule-2 completion is a matrix algebra $\Mat_2(\Cl^0(p,q))$ and so carries type P: the fusion's own matrix units supply the non-central idempotents and nilpotents. Transport never reaches a division algebra; each completion carries fresh obstructions of its own.
transport.no-transport-terminates.technical:
No algebra reachable by a nonempty transport history is free of zero divisors. A Rule 1 completion adjoins a hyperbolic plane, so its signature $(p+1, q+1)$ is mixed and it carries type N; indeed the adjoined pair satisfies $Q(f) = Q(f^{*}) = 0$, so the old null cone is repaired by adjoining new members of it.

A Rule 2 completion is $\Mat_2(\Cl^0(p,q))$, whose matrix units supply the non-central idempotent $E_{11}$ and the nonzero nilpotent $E_{12}$, so it carries type P. Transport never reaches a division algebra.
transport.no-transport-terminates.lay: Each repair in the transport programme enlarges the algebra to fix a failure of division. This result shows that the enlarged algebra always has failures of its own: one repair adds new light-like directions, the other produces projections and elements that square to zero. So the process never ends in an algebra where every nonzero element can be divided by.

transport.noinverse.formal: A null vector $v \neq 0$ has no left inverse and no right inverse in $\Cl(p,q)$, nor in any associative unital algebra containing $\Cl(p,q)$ as a unital subalgebra.
transport.noinverse.technical:
If $v \neq 0$ is null then $v^2 = Q(v) = 0$, and this relation persists in any associative unital algebra containing $\Cl(p,q)$ as a unital subalgebra, since the multiplication restricts. A right inverse with $vw = 1$ would give $v = v(vw) = v^2 w = 0$, and a left inverse with $wv = 1$ would give $v = (wv)v = w v^2 = 0$, both contradicting $v \neq 0$.

So no associative unital enlargement of the algebra can make a nonzero null vector invertible on either side.
transport.noinverse.lay: A null vector is a nonzero direction whose square is zero. Such an element can never be divided by: if it had an inverse on either side, multiplying through would force the vector itself to be zero. The argument uses only the fact that its square is zero, so it still applies in any larger algebra of the same kind that contains the original one.

proofs.main: The relation $v^2 = Q(v) = 0$ (\claimref{std-algebra.vector-squares}) persists in any algebra containing $\Cl(p,q)$ as a subalgebra, since the multiplication restricts. If $vw = 1$ then $v = v(vw) = v^2 w = 0$; if $wv = 1$ then $v = (wv)v = wv^2 = 0$. Either way a contradiction.

transport.obstructions-are-moved-never-d.formal: Proposition \claimref{transport.no-transport-terminates} is the zero-dimensional instance of a principle the transport programme repeatedly meets: a completion never removes degeneracy, it relocates it. We conjecture the following family form. For any family of quadratic forms degenerating tamely along a locus (in the sense of the series' sheaf-theoretic paper \cite{ButlerT4}), any completion of the family that is nondegenerate of constant signature on one side of the locus degenerates on a displaced locus on the other side; no completion is nondegenerate globally. The one-sided completion theorem and shadow wall of that paper prove exactly this for tame corank-one degenerations; the conjecture asserts the pattern is not an artefact of the tame case, and asks for the cohomological invariant that measures it, presumably a class built from the mod-8 residues on the two sides of the wall, the state machine of Proposition \claimref{transport.fusion-occurs-most-once} evaluated in families.
transport.obstructions-are-moved-never-d.technical:

The fact that no transport terminates is read as the zero-dimensional instance of a family statement: for any family of quadratic forms degenerating tamely along a locus, any completion that is nondegenerate of constant signature on one side of the locus degenerates on a displaced locus on the other side, so no completion is nondegenerate globally. The one-sided completion theorem and shadow wall of the sheaf paper prove this for tame corank-one degenerations.

The conjecture asserts that the pattern is not an artefact of that case, and asks for the cohomological invariant that measures it, presumably a class built from the mod-8 residues on the two sides of the wall.
transport.obstructions-are-moved-never-d.lay: Each repair of a failure of division seems to create a new failure somewhere else. This conjecture proposes that the same holds when the geometry varies from place to place: fixing a degeneration on one side of a boundary pushes it to a new boundary on the other side. It has been proved in the simplest cases, and the conjecture also asks what quantity keeps track of the moved obstruction.

transport.original-conjecture-refuted-be.formal: Division by zero promotes the element. For every null vector $v$ of $\Cl(p,q)$ there is, in the minimal ascent $\Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1)$, a canonically chosen partner $\sigma(v)$ satisfying $v\,\sigma(v)\,v = v$, the choice equivariant under the symmetries of the original algebra: the impossible division is repaired, element by element, one ascent up.
transport.original-conjecture-refuted-be.technical: For every null vector $v$ of $\Cl(p,q)$ one could hope for a partner $\sigma(v)$ in the minimal ascent $\Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1)$ with $v\,\sigma(v)\,v = v$, chosen equivariantly under the symmetries of the original algebra, so that the failed division is repaired element by element. The paper states this to refute it: no equivariant element-level partner exists, and the repair happens at the level of points instead.
transport.original-conjecture-refuted-be.lay: The first guess was that a vector you cannot divide by could be given a partner in a slightly larger algebra, one vector at a time, in a way that respects all the symmetries. That guess is wrong, and the series records it as refuted: the repair works for points of the geometry, not for individual elements.

transport.pair-canonical-label-bit.formal: For an idempotent $e \notin \{0,1\}$, set $u = 2e - 1$, an involution ($u^2 = 1$), with $e = \tfrac12(1+u)$ and $1 - e = \tfrac12(1-u)$ its spectral projections. The unordered pair $\{e, 1-e\}$ and the involution $\pm u$ determine one another canonically; the residual choice (which member to call $e$, equivalently the sign of $u$) is a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ labelling. By Theorem \claimref{transport.classification-idempotent-orbits}(2) this labelling is gauge (implemented by an inner automorphism) precisely for balanced pairs, and is canonically resolved by rank order otherwise. The pattern is now visible across the whole taxonomy: each obstruction type terminates in a residual $\mathbb{Z}_2$: the labelling of $\varepsilon_\pm$ for type C, exchangeable by no inner automorphism and rendered gauge only by the ascent (Proposition \claimref{transport.ascent-renders-grade-involution-inner}); the sign $\gamma$ of the fused ascent for Rule 2, not detected by the algebra (Remark \claimref{note.transport.bit-algebra-forgets}); and the labelling of $\{e, 1-e\}$ for type P, gauge already in the base algebra whenever the ranks permit. The three $\mathbb{Z}_2$'s are at strictly decreasing depth: outer, forgotten, inner.
transport.pair-canonical-label-bit.technical:
For an idempotent $e \notin \{0, 1\}$ the element $u = 2e - 1$ is an involution, $u^2 = 1$, with spectral projections $e = \tfrac12(1 + u)$ and $1 - e = \tfrac12(1 - u)$. The unordered pair $\{e, 1 - e\}$ and the involution $\pm u$ determine one another canonically, leaving a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ label: which member is called $e$, equivalently the sign of $u$. By the classification of idempotent orbits this label is gauge, implemented by an inner automorphism, exactly for balanced pairs, and is otherwise resolved by rank order.

Each obstruction type ends in such a $\mathbb{Z}_2$: for type C the labelling of $\varepsilon_\pm$, exchanged by no inner automorphism and made inner only by the ascent; for Rule 2 the sign of the fused ascent, which the algebra does not detect; for type P the labelling of $\{e, 1 - e\}$, inner already in the base whenever the ranks permit. The three sit at strictly decreasing depth: outer, forgotten, inner.
transport.pair-canonical-label-bit.lay: An element that equals its own square splits the space into two complementary parts, and that pair of parts is fixed without any choice. All that remains is a single yes-or-no choice of which part to call the first. Each of the three kinds of obstruction leaves such a bit, and the three bits are progressively easier to undo by a symmetry.

transport.pseudo-inverse-torsor.formal:
On $S(v)$ define $\sigma \sim \sigma'$ iff $\sigma - \sigma' \in v\,\Cl(\mathbb{V}')$, the left ideal generated by $v$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Each class contains a unique representative of the form $w_0 + \alpha$ with $\alpha \in \Cl(U')$, so the quotient $T(v) := S(v)/\!\sim$ is an affine space with translation space $\Cl(U')$, via $[w_0 + \alpha] + \xi = [w_0 + \alpha + \xi]$.
\item $N_v$ preserves $S(v)$ and the equivalence, hence acts on $T(v)$; the action is by translations along the grade-one subspace $U \subseteq \Cl(U')$:
\[
R_u \cdot [\,w_0 + \alpha\,] \;=\; [\,w_0 + \alpha - u\,].
\]
\item The $N_v$-orbit of any class is a torsor under $(U, +)$, and its translation cocycle, with respect to any base point, is the tautological homomorphism $\theta : N_v \to U$, $\theta(R_u) = u$.
\end{enumerate}
transport.pseudo-inverse-torsor.technical:
Let $S(v)$ be the set of pseudo-inverses of a null vector $v$ in $\Cl(\mathbb{V}')$, and set $\sigma \sim \sigma'$ when $\sigma - \sigma'$ lies in the left ideal $v\,\Cl(\mathbb{V}')$. Each class has a unique representative $w_0 + \alpha$ with $\alpha \in \Cl(U')$, so $T(v) = S(v)/{\sim}$ is an affine space with translation space $\Cl(U')$. The null rotations act on $T(v)$ by translation along the grade-one subspace $U$: $R_u \cdot [w_0 + \alpha] = [w_0 + \alpha - u]$.

Hence every $N_v$-orbit is a torsor under $(U, +)$, and its translation cocycle with respect to any base point is the tautological homomorphism $\theta(R_u) = u$.
transport.pseudo-inverse-torsor.lay: A light-like direction has many partial inverses. After discarding differences that do not matter, the remaining choices form a flat space, like a plane with no chosen origin. The symmetries that fix the light-like direction slide this space along itself, so, except in the smallest case where there is no extra direction to slide along, no choice is left unmoved.

transport.regularity-localises-zero-divi.formal:
Every semisimple Artinian ring, in particular every real Clifford algebra of nondegenerate form, is von Neumann regular. Consequently, if $a$ is a nonzero zero divisor in such a ring $A$, and $x$ satisfies $axa = a$, then $e = xa$ and $f = ax$ are idempotents with
\[
a(1 - e) = 0, \qquad (1 - f)a = 0, \qquad e, f \notin \{0, 1\}.
\]
Moreover $ae = a$ and $fa = a$.
transport.regularity-localises-zero-divi.technical: Every semisimple Artinian ring, in particular every real Clifford algebra of nondegenerate form, is von Neumann regular: each $a$ has some $x$ with $axa = a$. If $a$ is a nonzero zero divisor and $axa = a$, then $e = xa$ and $f = ax$ are idempotents with $a(1 - e) = 0$, $(1 - f)a = 0$ and $e, f \notin \{0, 1\}$; moreover $ae = a$ and $fa = a$.
transport.regularity-localises-zero-divi.lay: In the algebras of the series every element has a weak kind of inverse that undoes it partway. Applying that weak inverse to an element that cannot be divided by produces elements equal to their own squares, which pin down exactly where the failure sits. This is the step that turns every failure of division into a statement about such elements.
transport.regularity-localises-zero-divi.typing_note: Edge kept: the classification supplies semisimplicity; Wedderburn-Artin and von Neumann regularity are standard but proved in the paper, and no imported claim for them is in the store.

proofs.main: By Wedderburn--Artin a semisimple Artinian ring is a finite product of matrix rings over division rings, and it suffices to verify regularity in $\Mat_k(D)$: any matrix $a$ of rank $r$ can be written $a = u \begin{psmallmatrix} 1_r & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{psmallmatrix} v$ with $u, v$ invertible, and $x = v^{-1} \begin{psmallmatrix} 1_r & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix} u^{-1}$ gives $axa = a$. (Clifford algebras of nondegenerate forms are semisimple by Theorem \claimref{transport.classification-real-clifford-algebras}.) For the consequence: $e^2 = xaxa = xa = e$, and $a(1-e) = a - axa = 0$; symmetrically for $f$. Also $ae = axa = a$ and $fa = axa = a$. If $e = 1$ then $xa = 1$, so $a$ is left-invertible, hence invertible in an Artinian ring, contradicting that $a$ is a zero divisor; if $e = 0$ then $a = ae = 0$, contradicting $a \neq 0$. The same for $f$.

transport.splitting-along-hyperbolic-pla.formal:
Let $\mathbb{V}' = H_0 \perp U'$ be an orthogonal decomposition with $H_0$ a hyperbolic plane spanned by a hyperbolic pair $(v, w_0)$; the form on $U'$ may be degenerate. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\{1, v, w_0, v w_0\}$ is a linear basis of $\Cl(H_0)$, and every element of $\Cl(\mathbb{V}')$ admits a \emph{unique} expansion
\[
\sigma \;=\; \alpha + v\beta + w_0\gamma + v w_0\,\delta, \qquad \alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta \in \Cl(U').
\]
\item Left multiplication by $v$ is injective on $\Cl(U')$.
\end{enumerate}
transport.splitting-along-hyperbolic-pla.technical: Let $\mathbb{V}' = H_0 \perp U'$ with $H_0$ the hyperbolic plane spanned by a hyperbolic pair $(v, w_0)$, the form on $U'$ possibly degenerate. Moreover, left multiplication by $v$ is injective on $\Cl(U')$.

transport.type-p-self-repairing.formal:
Let $A$ be any unital ring, $\mathcal{E}(A)$ its set of idempotents, and $A' \supseteq A$ any unital extension. The identity assignment
\[
\sigma : \mathcal{E}(A) \to A' , \qquad \sigma(e) = e,
\]
satisfies both von Neumann identities, $e\,\sigma(e)\,e = e$ and $\sigma(e)\,e\,\sigma(e) = \sigma(e)$, and is equivariant under \emph{every} ring automorphism of every extension: for any automorphism $\theta$ of $A'$ preserving $A$, $\sigma(\theta(e)) = \theta(\sigma(e))$ trivially. In the terminology of the taxonomy: the transport rule for type P is the identity, at signature increment $(0,0)$, and the repair is already present in the base algebra.
transport.type-p-self-repairing.technical:
Let $A$ be any unital ring, $\mathcal{E}(A)$ its idempotents and $A' \supseteq A$ any unital extension. Taking each idempotent as its own partner, $\sigma(e) = e$, both von Neumann identities $e\,\sigma(e)\,e = e$ and $\sigma(e)\,e\,\sigma(e) = \sigma(e)$ hold because $e^3 = e$. The assignment commutes with every automorphism $\theta$ of $A'$ preserving $A$, since $\theta(e)$ is again an idempotent of $A$ and $\sigma$ is the identity.

In the obstruction taxonomy this says that the transport rule for type P, the non-central idempotents, is the identity at signature increment $(0,0)$: the repair is already present in the base algebra.
transport.type-p-self-repairing.lay: Some zero divisors are projection-like elements, ones that equal their own square. For these, the repair being sought is already available: each such element can serve as its own partner and satisfies the required identities. Because the rule is simply to take the element itself, it automatically respects every symmetry, so nothing needs to be added to the algebra.

transport.units-span.formal: In a finite-dimensional unital $\R$-algebra $A$, every element is a sum of two invertible elements.
transport.units-span.technical: In a finite-dimensional unital $\R$-algebra $A$ every element is a sum of two invertible elements. For $a \in A$, the element $a - \lambda 1$ fails to be invertible only for the finitely many real $\lambda$ with $\det(L_a - \lambda\,\mathrm{id}) = 0$, so some $\lambda \neq 0$ makes both $a - \lambda 1$ and $\lambda 1$ invertible, and $a = (a - \lambda 1) + \lambda 1$.
transport.units-span.lay: In any finite-dimensional algebra over the real numbers, even an element that cannot be divided by is the sum of two elements that can. The trick is to subtract a suitable multiple of 1, which leaves something invertible for all but finitely many choices.
transport.units-span.typing_note: No premises: the proof is self-contained linear algebra.

proofs.main: For $a \in A$ and $\lambda \in \R$, the element $a - \lambda 1$ is invertible iff the left-multiplication operator $L_a - \lambda\, \mathrm{id}$ on the finite-dimensional space $A$ is invertible (if $L_{a - \lambda 1}$ is bijective, the preimage of $1$ is a right inverse, and finite-dimensionality upgrades one-sided inverses to two-sided). The reals $\lambda$ for which $\det(L_a - \lambda\,\mathrm{id}) = 0$ are finitely many, so choose $\lambda$ with both $a - \lambda 1$ and $\lambda 1$ invertible ($\lambda \neq 0$): then $a = (a - \lambda 1) + \lambda 1$.

transport.where-obstruction-lies-commuti.formal:
Let $A = \Cl(p,q)$ with $n = p + q$ even, and let $A_s = \Cl(p,q{+}1)$ and $A_t = \Cl(p{+}1,q)$ be its spacelike and timelike one-dimensional extensions.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Exactly one of $A_s$, $A_t$ carries the type-C obstruction: $A_s$ if $p - q \equiv 2 \pmod 4$, $A_t$ if $p - q \equiv 0 \pmod 4$. The other has complex type: its volume element is central with square $-1$, its centre is $\C$, and it is simple.
\item[(b)] Each of the two ideals of the obstructed extension is a copy of $A$: $\varepsilon_\pm A_s \cong \Cl^0(p,q{+}1) \cong A$ in the first case, $\varepsilon_\pm A_t \cong \Cl^0(p{+}1,q) \cong \Cl(q,p) \cong A$ in the second (the last isomorphism because the residues $0$ and $4$ are fixed by negation mod $8$).
\item[(c)] The Rule 2 repair of the obstructed extension by a generator of the opposite sign is $\Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1)$, the Rule 1 ascent of $A$: the two adjoined generators $e_{n+1}$ (the extension) and $\nu$ (the repair) span a hyperbolic plane, the null vectors $f = \tfrac12(u \pm w)$, $f^* = \tfrac12(u \mp w)$, with $u$ the adjoined generator of square $+1$ and $w$ that of square $-1$ (both combinations are null; the opposite signs make $ff^* + f^*f = 1$) are the ladder pair of Theorem \claimref{transport.rule-1-morita-trivial}, and the two amplifications agree: $\Mat_2(\Cl^0(\text{extension})) = \Mat_2(A)$. For an even-dimensional $\Cl(p,q)$ with residue $d = p - q \bmod 8$, the spacelike one-dimensional extension carries the type-C obstruction exactly when $d \in \{2, 6\}$ and the timelike one exactly when $d \in \{0, 4\}$, so every even residue has exactly one obstructing one-dimensional extension. Using that Rule 1 ascents preserve the residue, the physical lineage at $d = 6$ leaves residue $6$ only through a spacelike Kaluza-Klein direction, into the type-C obstruction at residue $5$.

The Rule 2 repair of that obstruction by a generator of the opposite sign returns it to residue $6$ as $\Mat_2$ of the algebra it started from. The mirror residue $2$ behaves in the same way when spacelike means square $-1$; in T14's causal convention that obstructing extension is the mirror's second time, not its Kaluza-Klein direction.
transport.which-residues-obstruct-which-.lay: Clifford algebras repeat in a cycle of eight, so each one has a residue from 0 to 7. For the even residues, adding one new space direction breaks the algebra into two pieces exactly at residues 2 and 6, and adding one new time direction does so exactly at 0 and 4. The physical case sits at residue 6: its only exit is an extra space direction, and repairing that break with a direction of the opposite kind brings it back to residue 6 as two-by-two matrices over where it began.
